The results reveal a complex picture of perceptions, with evidence suggesting the equation of NES identity with specific nationalities, ethno-cultural backgrounds, physical attributes and linguistic and pedagogic competencies. The EFA yielded a four-factor solution, representing distinct aspects of the NES identity, namely, national identity of NES, requirements to be NES, features of NES and home country of NES. The findings indicate a persistent multi-faceted influence of native-speakerism ideology on the construction of the NES identity, showing that it is strongly associated with Anglophonic nationalities, European descent and linguistic superiority. However, some results reveal open-minded views about the NES identity, recognising its potential fluidity. Overall, the study contributes to discussions on language ideologies and contemporary perspectives on English nativeness, challenging simplistic categorisations based solely on language ability and highlighting the complexity with which language perceptions are expressed.

title: Participation as shared responsibility in industrial heritage management
abstract: Abstract Participation (from citizens, stakeholders, etc.) is often necessary when managing industrial heritage. In this conceptual paper, we will argue that, in this context, participation should generally be understood as shared responsibility. We will present our argument in three stages. Firstly, we will introduce the concept of shared responsibility in planning. To illustrate how this works in practice, we will use the Australian National Strategy for Disaster Resilience (NSDR) as a paradigm. Building on this, we will introduce the idea of shared responsibility in more detail. Secondly, we will analyse how participation is understood in key approaches to heritage management and planning (Critical heritage perspective of the authorised heritage discourse; Collaborative planning; Sustainable development; Governing the commons). Thirdly and finally, we will demonstrate that, while these approaches are compatible with a shared-responsibility model, they are less suitable when the specific characteristics of industrial heritage management are taken into account (such as multi-level governance structures). In conclusion, qualified (‘inclusive’) participation can be understood as the differentiated, multi-level, task-oriented sharing of responsibility (whether paid or voluntary) between, on the one hand, professional or ‘authorised’ actors, and, on the other hand, local ‘system’ experts and/or representatives (who may be elected or self-organised).

title: Targeted poverty alleviation and energy poverty in China’s rural households
abstract: Energy poverty is a significant global issue that has attracted extensive scholarly attention. In 2020, China successfully eradicated absolute income poverty, making a substantial contribution to global poverty reduction efforts. The correlation between energy poverty and income poverty is highly significant. Has China’s targeted poverty alleviation contributed to the elimination of energy poverty? Based on data from China Family Panel Studies covering the years 2012 to 2020, this study employs a difference-in-differences methodology, revealing that the implementation of targeted poverty alleviation has resulted in a statistically significant decrease in household energy poverty. Specifically, the energy burden ratio (EP1) falls by 15.4 percentage points; the probability of being energy poor under the 10% threshold (EP2) falls by 23.4 percentage points; the low-income high-cost measure (EP3) falls by 25.3 percentage points; the multidimensional energy poverty index (EP4) falls by 0.244; and the composite index (EP5) falls by 0.053 in absolute terms. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the energy poverty reduction effect of targeted poverty alleviation is more prominent in the central region of China and in households with school-age children. However, the energy poverty reduction effect is relatively weaker in households with elderly members or individuals hospitalized due to illness. Mechanism analysis indicates that targeted poverty alleviation can promote employment, increase disposable income, and enhance the affordability of household energy. In addition, targeted poverty alleviation measures also alleviate energy poverty by improving household energy consumption structure, raising environmental awareness, and promoting more adoption of energy-saving appliances in households. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for other developing countries facing similar challenges in addressing energy poverty and promoting sustainable development.

title: Branding the bull: brand attraction on stock volatility and returns in the developed and emerging markets
abstract: This study examines how brand attraction influences stock returns and stock volatility, and how investor sentiment moderates these relationships across developed and emerging markets. Using panel data from 5,281 publicly listed firms in the United States, China, and India from January 2018 to June 2025, fixed-effects and feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) estimations are employed to account for firm-level heterogeneity and time-series dependence. The empirical results show that higher brand attraction is consistently associated with higher stock returns, indicating that brand visibility functions as a value-relevant signal in financial markets. At the same time, brand attraction significantly increases stock volatility, reflecting intensified investor attention and trading activity. Investor sentiment plays a critical moderating role by amplifying both returns and volatility, with interaction effects substantially stronger in China and India than in the United States. This cross-market heterogeneity suggests that sentiment-driven amplification is more pronounced in environments characterised by greater information asymmetry and higher retail investor participation. This study makes a novel contribution by empirically demonstrating that brand attraction simultaneously affects market performance and risk, and by providing cross-country evidence that investor sentiment is a key channel through which brand-related information is amplified in emerging markets.

title: The impact of environmental policy on corporate greenwashing behavior from the perspective of multiple institutional logics
abstract: Corporate greenwashing behavior has become an obstacle to environmental, economic and social development. Limiting corporate greenwashing through environmental policy and encouraging companies to participate in environmental governance have become effective ways to promote sustainable development. From the perspective of multiple institutional logics, this paper constructs an analytical framework for examining the relationship between environmental policy and corporate greenwashing behavior based on regulation logics, and explores the moderating role of public environmental awareness and performance aspiration gap by identifying ecological community logic and efficiency logic. This paper examines heavily polluting listed companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen A-share markets. An empirical test was conducted using Stata17.0 software. The results indicate an inverted U-shaped relationship between punitive environmental policy and corporate greenwashing behavior, while incentive environmental policy has a positive impact on corporate greenwashing behavior. Second, public environmental awareness weakens the inverted U-shaped relationship between punitive environmental policy and corporate greenwashing behavior. Third, performance aspiration gap strengthens the positive relationship between incentive environmental policy and corporate greenwashing behavior. This paper suggests that effective implementation of environmental policy is crucial in preventing greenwashing, and external regulation and internal performance concerns are important in supporting the role of environmental policy.

title: The relationship between social media use and materialism: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis
abstract: The widespread use of social media increases the likelihood of exposure to materialistic content, prompting extensive research into the relationship between social media use (SMU) and materialism. However, a comprehensive quantitative synthesis of this relationship remains lacking. This study conducted a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis to examine the association between SMU and materialism, and to assess whether the association varies across SMU types, materialism measurements, and sample characteristics. A total of 55 studies, encompassing 90 effect sizes and 28,531 participants, were included through a systematic literature search. The results showed a significant positive association between SMU and materialism ( r = 0.322). SMU type, culture, and materialism measure significantly moderated this association, whereas country income, gender, and age were not significant moderators. These findings highlight the need to consider measures that promote diverse, non-materialistic social media content and enhance users’ media literacy, which may help mitigate materialistic orientations.

title: Physical traces: Aesthetics of care and the picturebook as a nature/culture product
abstract: While publishers, educators and academics have been grappling with the impacts of digital media on children’s publishing, another trend has quietly emerged on bookshelves in the children’s section of the library. Ironically, given print picturebooks’ once-prophesised extinction, their very haptic qualities of the paper picturebook have surged, with trade publishers making concerted efforts to emphasise the medium’s materiality. From a wider range of textured paper stock to increasingly sophisticated paper engineering techniques, and the use of vegetable-based inks that emanate a patent scent, the picturebooks in our children’s hands have become extraordinary, material story objects. The reasons behind enhanced materiality in a digital age are not merely aesthetic or market driven. This paper contributes to the existing research on picturebook haptics by thinking through their presence in the context of rising climate catastrophe and ecoanxiety. We suggest the materiality of such works have the potential to present a posthuman challenge beyond the digitisation of children’s literature. We argue the ‘thingness’ of a printed picturebook can offer children an encounter with the more-than-human. That is, while a child engages in the narrative world of their book-as-object, they are also engaging in an embodied and embedded subjectivity consistent with Josephine Donovan’s conceptions of an aesthetics of care: one that is literal, agentic, materialist, entangled and vitalist, firmly grounded in a specific sense of place and the lived experience of the other. Further, we situate these theoretical interrogations within reflections on making and practice, and the limitations and challenges present in this pursuit. To innovatively embody the I-Thou aesthetic of care Donovan advocates, we collaborate on this discussion from the subject positions of an ecocritical reader and eco-motivated creator-illustrator to consider the meaning making and sustainability of our relationships with the non-human in the material, visual and verbal modalities of the 2012 award-winning picturebook The Boy Who Grew Into a Tree .

title: Climate change beliefs, reasons for migration and public support for immigrants: evidence from a vignette experiment
abstract: Abstract Ongoing global conflicts and the accelerating effects of climate change are expected to intensify migration flows, underscoring the importance of understanding public attitudes toward immigrants. Research suggests that attitudes toward accepting immigrants vary depending on the reason for migration and, relatedly, their perceived deservingness. Refugees fleeing political persecution or war generally receive higher public support than economic migrants, while attitudes toward climate change-induced migration remain more ambiguous, probably partly reflecting the ambiguities surrounding this category in international law. Previous studies also suggest that some types of environmental attitudes may be related to the acceptance of climate change-induced immigrants. This study examines how climate change beliefs relate to support for admitting immigrants and whether this association varies by the reason for migration. We conducted a survey experiment with 1477 randomly selected respondents in the Czech Republic, a country with historically low levels of immigration and ethnic diversity, which recently experienced an unprecedented influx of war refugees from Ukraine. Respondents evaluated whether a hypothetical immigrant should be admitted to the country. The vignette randomly varied the stated reason for migration: no reason given, political persecution, religious discrimination, economic hardship, climate change, or war. The results indicate that support for admission was highest for migrants fleeing political or religious persecution, while climate migrants received the lowest level of support, and the gap widened among respondents who rejected anthropogenic climate change. Belief in human-caused climate change was positively associated with support for admitting immigrants in general and especially climate migrants, consistent with the deservingness logic (greater perceived need and lower perceived control) and with the idea that climate scepticism clusters with anti-immigration orientations. Findings suggest that climate beliefs may shape the perceived deservingness of migrants and that the politicisation of climate change could hinder public acceptance of people displaced by environmental factors.

title: Can care from adult children reduce elderly healthcare expenditures? Evidence from China
abstract: Abstract This study uses the 2016–2022 waves of the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) to examine how care from adult children affects elderly healthcare expenditures, with a focus on the moderating role of social care services. Three key findings emerge. First, care from adult children significantly reduces medical expenses by improving health monitoring, nutrition, and health behaviors—acting as a substitute for formal healthcare. This result holds under multiple robustness checks. Second, this effect operates primarily through the promotion of healthy lifestyles, improved management of chronic diseases, and enhanced psychological outlook, thereby strengthening the overall health status of older adults. Additionally, heterogeneous effects show that the benefits of caregiving are stronger among lower- and middle-income households, families where mothers are the primary care recipients, and particularly among disabled elderly individuals—highlighting how economic vulnerability, gendered family roles, and functional health status jointly shape the dynamics and impact of intergenerational care. Third, increased access to social care services (e.g., institutional beds and community-based programs) strengthens rather than weakens the effectiveness of family caregiving, indicating a complementary relationship between formal and informal care. In areas with greater institutional capacity, formal systems help relieve routine and high-intensity tasks, enabling family members to focus on emotional support and health management. This coordination enhances the overall efficiency of eldercare and leads to greater reductions in healthcare expenditures. These findings highlight that formal and informal care function as mutually reinforcing components of an integrated care system, offering both theoretical insight and policy relevance for promoting sustainable eldercare in aging societies.

title: CSR and profitability mediated by the cost of debt: a new look at Scandinavian manufacturing companies
abstract: This study examines the impact of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) on firm profitability for the Scandinavian region known for its strong CSR engagement. Using Return on Assets (ROA) as a measure of profitability, the study employs fixed effect panel study method as well as GMM IV method. The findings indicate a statistically significant and positive relationship between CSR practices, measured by Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores, and firm profitability (ROA). Firms with higher ESG scores experience improved profitability, which, in turn, enhances opportunities for further CSR investments. Additionally, the study identifies cost of debt as a key mediating factor in the CSR-profitability relationship. Lower cost of debt is associated with stronger CSR performance, further reinforcing profitability. These findings suggest that CSR does not only contribute to societal well-being but it enhances financial outcomes, especially for manufacturing companies that are more waste producing and hence, investors would be more sensitive to their CSR practices. As a result, CSR serves as a strategic tool for sustainable corporate growth. The study provides insights for managers, investors, and policymakers.

title: The long shadow of famine: CEO early-life experience and corporate ESG
abstract: Despite the growing institutionalization of ESG and the constraints imposed by high transparency, firms continue to exhibit substantial heterogeneity in sustainable governance. Through the lens of managers’ early-life experiences, this paper uses a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms to examine the effect of CEOs’ exposure to the Great Chinese Famine on corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. We find that firms led by famine-exposed CEOs have significantly lower ESG scores, with an average decline of 2.91%. Further analyses show that this negative effect is stronger when CEOs have longer career horizons and when the executive team is more homogeneous in famine exposure, but weaker when industry peers exhibit higher ESG performance, suggesting that benchmarking and normative pressure can partially discipline governance deviations rooted in managerial heterogeneity.

title: An explainable machine learning framework linking ESG performance and supply chain resilience prediction: evidence from Chinese listed companies
abstract: Supply Chain Resilience (SCR) has become a strategic capability for firms facing increasing uncertainty. However, the vast majority of existing research falls into an “ex-post explanation” paradigm, which focuses on retrospective attribution analysis of realized shock outcomes or treats resilience merely as a static outcome variable. This paradigm fails to meet the urgent needs of firms for ex-ante risk early warning and capability assessment in uncertain environments. To fill this gap, this study develops an explainable machine-learning framework to predict resilience using downside-risk-based labels and comprehensive firm characteristics. “Using a comprehensive panel dataset of Chinese A-share listed companies spanning raw operational data from 2010 to 2023 (with predictive modeling evaluated on 2014–2023 labels), this study integrates financial flexibility, supply-chain structure, corporate governance, and ESG performance into multiple machine-learning models, among which XGBoost demonstrates the strongest predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.868). SHAP analysis further reveals heterogeneous and nonlinear mechanisms underlying resilience formation. Crucially, the model uncovers an internal hierarchy within the ESG framework: Governance (G) explicitly dominates Environmental (E) and Social (S) dimensions as the primary predictor of crisis survival. Specifically, governance quality and institutional ownership are associated with strong monotonic increases in predicted resilience, acting as immediate risk-governance mechanisms, whereas E and S factors serve as latent reputational buffers. Furthermore, liquidity shows diminishing marginal predictive contributions, and customer concentration has a U-shaped relationship driven by strategic dependence versus vulnerability. These findings broaden theoretical insights into the ESG–resilience nexus and highlight the necessity of balancing governance discipline, financial adaptability, and relational coordination to enhance organizational resilience. The research contributes a transparent and forward-looking decision-support tool for firms and policymakers who seek to improve resilience under evolving supply-chain risks.

title: What comes after voicing: understanding the drivers of immobility and strategies for coping with a dissatisfying status quo
abstract: Existing literature often conceptualises emigration as a response to dissatisfaction with the societal status quo, particularly when attempts to voice change are perceived as ineffective. Yet, even under conditions of dissatisfaction and increasing feasibility of movement, the majority of people do not migrate. This raises a fundamental but relatively underexplored question of why people stay, highlighting the need to advance and refine our conceptualisation of immobility. Our study provides insights into this question by drawing on post-2019 Hong Kong. We conducted in-depth interviews with 24 adult Hong Kong residents who participated in the 2019 social movement (a manifestation of dissatisfaction) but remained in the city five years after the event. We examine their drivers of immobility and strategies for coping with a dissatisfying status quo. Low readiness due to personal accumulated investments and strained financial circumstances emerged as key drivers of involuntary immobility. Voluntary immobility was driven by factors including perceived economic opportunities and embeddedness in the home context, concerns about language barriers and discrimination at potential destinations, and not yet having started a family. These observations suggest that migration intentions are not static. We also identified responses to dissatisfaction beyond physical departure (i.e. emigration). Neglect and goal adjustment were observed among involuntary stayers, while compliance was observed among voluntary stayers. We discussed their implications to the literature.

title: The associations of AI-integrated entrepreneurship education versus traditional entrepreneurship education on undergraduates’ entrepreneurial intention and its antecedents
abstract: This study investigates the differential associations between AI-integrated entrepreneurship education (AIEE), traditional entrepreneurship education (TEE), and college students’ entrepreneurial intention (EI) using survey data collected from a university in Suzhou, China. Adopting a quasi-experimental design with two intact classes, the present research cannot disentangle the standalone effect of AI tools from the full instructional package. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and the Entrepreneurial Potential Model (EPM), this research compares path strength differences and group-specific indirect effects across AIEE and TEE groups, focusing on entrepreneurial attitudes (ATE), subjective norms (SN), perceived behavioral control (PBC), perceived desirability (PD), and perceived feasibility (PF). Multi-group partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) results based on 133 valid participants (AIEE: n = 68; TEE: n = 65) reveal that paths from ATE and PBC to EI, alongside the group-specific indirect effects via PD and PF, are significantly stronger in the AIEE group. This work provides small-scale quasi-experimental evidence for contextual entrepreneurship education research. Due to non-random class assignment, single-site sampling, cross-sectional data, unmeasured confounders, and the inability to isolate pure AI effects, all findings are interpreted as correlational rather than causal, offering actionable implications for the iterative optimization of entrepreneurship curricula.

title: Community of inquiry as a zone of proximal development: cultivating English-as-a-foreign-language students’ discussion performance
abstract: Existing empirical studies in first language contexts have demonstrated that Lipman’s community of inquiry (CoI) approach fosters students’ critical thinking, creative thinking, communication, and collaboration. However, its impact in English as a foreign language (EFL) settings remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by investigating how integrating the CoI approach in an EFL university classroom affects students’ discussion performance, particularly in terms of participation, interaction, and cognition. Fifteen second-year EFL students participated in an eleven-week intervention, during which seven hours of video from eleven CoI discussions were collected. Content analysis of the discussion transcripts focused on turn-taking, interaction patterns, and cognitive depth. The findings revealed that students’ turn-taking percentage increased from 66.70% to 75.90% and that the spoken word percentage grew from 60.80% to 84.80%. Later CoI discussions featured more synergistic interactions and deeper cognitive engagement. Specifically, basic ‘exploration’ decreased by more than half, whereas in-depth ‘integration’ increased by a similar degree by the end of the intervention. An intimate relationship between in-depth cognition and synergistic interaction also emerged. These findings suggest that the CoI approach can potentially increase EFL students’ participation, interaction, and cognition, offering pedagogical, theoretical, and methodological implications for teachers and researchers in China and comparable contexts. The limitations of this study are acknowledged, and suggestions for future research are provided.

title: Subtitling the self: algorithmic governance and dialectal counter-logics in Arabic media localization
abstract: This paper presents an empirical, computationally grounded investigation of Arabic audiovisual translation as a contested field of algorithmic governance. Focusing on Netflix’s localization pipelines and their encounter with the Syrian Arabic dialect—the dominant infrastructure of grassroots translation for Turkish and Mexican television drama series—we argue that corporate, community, and machine translation systems operate according to fundamentally different optimization functions. Through a mixed-methods framework that applies algorithmized analysis to a triangulated corpus, we develop and apply four key computational metrics: the Syrian Dialect Divergence Score (S-DDS), Syrian Lexical Richness Score (SLRS), Cultural Proximity via Embedding Alignment, and Contextual Sentiment Accuracy (CSA). Our findings demonstrate that corporate localization systematically neutralizes dialectal markedness (SLRS: 0.02–0.05), fan communities strategically maximize it (SLRS: 0.15–0.30, S-DDS: 0.6–0.8), and current machine translation systems are structurally incapable of engaging with Syrian Arabic’s socio-pragmatic depth. The paper concludes that Syrian Arabic functions not merely as a linguistic variant but as a form of cultural counter-algorithm—a human, dialectally embedded system of affective and cultural intelligence that exposes the limitations of platform-based localization governed by risk minimization and standardization. This research contributes to Translation Studies, Arabic Sociolinguistics, and media platform studies by providing an empirical model for analyzing the politics of dialect in digital cultural exchange.

title: Examining ChatGPT-supported speaking practice among Saudi EFL students: a quasi-experimental study
abstract: Speaking remains a persistent challenge for Saudi EFL learners, as large classes, limited exposure, and speaking anxiety restrict opportunities for practice. This quasi-experimental study examined whether ChatGPT-supported speaking practice was associated with higher adjusted post-test oral proficiency scores than those obtained with traditional instruction. Two intact groups of undergraduates ( N = 42) participated over twelve weeks: an experimental group ( n = 20) engaged in typed ChatGPT-supported conversational scaffolding integrated with spoken classroom role-play and task-based oral production, while a control group ( n = 22) followed conventional instruction. Speaking performance was assessed using a validated analytic rubric covering eight criteria: fluency, pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, coherence and organisation, interaction and engagement, task completion, and delivery and intelligibility. A significant baseline difference between groups was observed; therefore, analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was used to evaluate post-test performance while controlling for pre-test proficiency. After adjustment, the experimental group achieved higher overall speaking scores than the control group ( p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.60). Descriptive patterns across rubric dimensions suggested broader improvements in oral performance. The combination of typed ChatGPT-supported scaffolding, immediate feedback, structured speaking tasks, and teacher-mediated interaction may have increased opportunities for oral production in classroom contexts. The findings suggest that guided use of ChatGPT can complement traditional instruction and support the development of EFL speaking performance in higher education settings.

title: The role of corporate social responsibility in promoting community development for the Hormuud Salaam Foundation in Mogadishu, Somalia
abstract: Corporate Social Responsibility increasingly shapes development outcomes in fragile and conflict-affected contexts where public institutions face capacity constraints. This study investigates the relationship between Corporate Social Responsibility initiatives and perceived community development outcomes using evidence from the Hormuud Salaam Foundation in Mogadishu, Somalia. Guided by stakeholder theory, the analysis focuses on three CSR dimensions: education and healthcare, job creation, and humanitarian and emergency support. A quantitative, cross-sectional, descriptive-correlational design was employed. Data were collected through structured questionnaires from 80 respondents, including managers, employees, and beneficiaries of the Foundation. Descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation analyses were used to examine associations between CSR dimensions and community development indicators. The results reveal strong and statistically significant positive relationships across all CSR dimensions. Humanitarian and emergency support demonstrated the strongest association with perceived community development (r = 0.877, p < 0.01), reflecting the importance of crisis response in Somalia’s fragile environment. Job creation initiatives were also strongly associated with community development (r = 0.860, p < 0.01), particularly in relation to economic empowerment and livelihood improvement, although perceptions of unemployment reduction were moderated by broader structural constraints. Education and healthcare initiatives showed a strong positive relationship with community development outcomes (r = 0.797, p < 0.01), highlighting their contribution to human-capital development, while concerns regarding equitable access to scholarships were identified. The study contributes empirical evidence from a conflict-affected setting, extending stakeholder theory by illustrating how domestic corporate foundations can complement weak state capacity. The findings underscore the importance of integrating humanitarian assistance with long-term development-oriented CSR strategies to enhance resilience, legitimacy, and sustainable community outcomes.

title: Political connections and firm export during institutional transition: evidence from Chinese private firms
abstract: Political connections influence firms’ international activities by changing their ability to negotiate with governments. Previous research has investigated the role PCs play in firms’ export but has failed to analyse the heterogeneity of PCs. This research disentangles the role that different types of PCs play in the PC-export relationship. Drawing on resource dependence theory and using a sample of 3586 firm-year observations from 1008 firms between 2008 and 2013, we find that the board of directors’ PCs negatively influence firms’ export. Exploration of the boundary conditions of the PCs-export relationship reveals that this negative impact is mainly caused by executive, as opposed to legislative PCs. We also find that the negative relationship between PCs and firm export is weakened when there is a broader range of PCs at different administrative levels among the board. This paper offers managerial insights for Chinese private firms developing their export strategies.

title: Media use and corruption perceptions: the mediating role of political trust and moderating role of group differences
abstract: Abstract Although media use has long played a central role in research on political attitudes, its relationship with corruption perceptions remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on the Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (DSMM), this study uses data from the seventh wave of the World Values Survey to examine how traditional and digital media use are associated with corruption perceptions, with political trust modeled as a mediating mechanism. It further investigates whether these pathways differ by gender, education, and settlement type. The findings reveal a differentiated pattern of media effects. Traditional media use is not directly associated with corruption perceptions, but is linked to lower perceived corruption through higher political trust. Digital media use is directly associated with higher perceived corruption, and also indirectly linked to higher perceived corruption through lower political trust. The multi-group analyses further show that the trust-mediated pathway linking digital media use to corruption is stronger among men, whereas the direct association between digital media use and corruption perceptions is more pronounced among less-educated respondents. No significant settlement-type differences were found in the digital media pathways, and no significant gender, education, or settlement-type differences were found in the traditional media pathways. By extending the DSMM framework to the study of corruption perceptions, this research highlights differentiated media-effect pathways across media types and audience groups, and contributes to research on mediated political cognition and offers implications for understanding how media environments, political trust, and anti-corruption governance intersect in contemporary China.

title: How does ESG shape corporate green innovation? A comprehensive review based on bibliometric and systematic literature analysis
abstract: Abstract Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) has become a key concept in sustainable development and is receiving growing attention. However, the relationship between ESG performances and corporate green innovation remains insufficiently explored. Guided by sustainable principles, firms are transitioning from profit-oriented models to value-driven strategies. This shift brings fundamental changes to their competitive logic and advantages, necessitating a theoretical re-evaluation of the factors driving corporate innovation. Given the interdisciplinary nature of ESG and GI, traditional literature review methods may fail to offer a comprehensive overview. This study employs bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review to examine the evolution, research trends, and knowledge structure of ESG and GI. Using CiteSpace, this study analysed 792 articles from the Web of Science Core Collection (2008–2024.10), revealing that research in this domain has entered a phase of rapid growth and has attracted considerable attention from international journals. Major contributions come from China, the UK and the US, yet international collaboration needs improvement. Core research themes include “sustainable development” “corporate social responsibility (CSR)” and “firm performance” while emerging trends focus on “Media Attention” “Green Technological Innovation” and “Green Investment.” Subsequently, the systematic literature analysis reveals that the influence of ESG on green innovation constitutes a complex, multi-layered interactive system, shaped primarily by mediating, moderating, and contextual factors. Mediating mechanisms facilitate green innovation by optimizing resource allocation, alleviating financing constraints, and strengthening stakeholder trust. Moderating factors such as environmental policies, executive characteristics, and market competition serve a critical regulatory function within this system. Additionally, contextual factors, including industry and firm characteristics, as well as internal and external environments, further enhance the applicability and relevance of the proposed framework. This study offers a comprehensive and systematic overview of the integration of ESG and GI, which may provide useful insights for future research and potentially contribute to corporate green transformation and the pursuit of sustainability goals.

title: Do ESG sub-dimensions strengthen market resilience during periods of socioeconomic uncertainty? Evidence from Borsa Istanbul
abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria have gained prominence in financial markets as sustainability indices have expanded worldwide. However, the extent to which ESG sub-dimensions are associated with different financial market indicators remains uncertain, especially in emerging markets marked by macroeconomic instability. Previous studies often rely on composite ESG scores and predominantly linear models, whereas this study examines the association between ESG sub-dimensions and three financial outcomes—stock prices, stock returns, and systematic market risk—for 23 firms listed in the Borsa Istanbul Sustainability Index. By applying nonlinear ensemble learning methods (XGBoost and Random Forest), the study evaluates the relative importance of ESG metrics alongside firm-specific and macroeconomic factors under baseline and crisis-augmented model specifications. The results reveal heterogeneous patterns across financial outcomes. Governance emerges as a key ESG-related variable in the price models, while environmental and governance dimensions are more closely associated with systematic market risk. In contrast, stock return dynamics are more strongly related to macroeconomic factors and episodic shocks, particularly during crisis periods. Overall, the findings suggest that ESG sub-dimensions are more consistently associated with firms’ structural exposure to systematic market risk and valuation indicators than with short-term return fluctuations.

title: The evolution of academic discourse on integrative innovation talent: a configurational analysis using fsQCA
abstract: Cultivating integrative innovation talent is a critical imperative for national competitive advantage in an era of complex innovation ecosystems. However, academic literature lacks a systematic, configuration-based understanding of the combinatorial pathways that foster such talent, often focusing on single factors rather than synergistic configurations. This study addresses this gap by uniquely treating academic discourse itself as the unit of analysis to map the evolution of this key knowledge domain. To this end, the study is explicitly positioned as a context-specific mapping of the Chinese academic discourse, aiming to reveal how the scholarly community of a major innovation-driven nation constructs successful narratives of talent development. We employ a novel methodological framework integrating scientometrics, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) on a corpus of 152 Chinese academic articles (2003–2023). Our fsQCA identifies multiple, equifinal configurations that are discursively constructed as successful, while our LDA excavates the core thematic substance underpinning this positive discourse. The study’s core finding reveals a significant temporal evolution in these discursive models: earlier literature (2003–2018) emphasizes “Demand for Talent” configurations, whereas recent discourse (2019-2023) converges on the centrality of “Interdisciplinary Training” as a core, almost self-sufficient, “capability-centered” configuration. This research contributes a structured, configurational map of a key knowledge domain’s cognitive evolution, offering an evidence-based framework that serves as a nuanced reference for policymakers and educators to understand discursive shifts within the scholarly community.

title: Complexity and dynamicity in the lexical richness of CSL learners: a longitudinal case study
abstract: Lexical richness is a critical dimension for measuring Chinese as a second language writing quality. The existing literature chiefly discusses the synchronic characteristics of Chinese lexical richness, while paying less attention to its dynamic development and longitudinal changes. Based on Dynamic Systems Theory, this empirical research investigates the diachronic features of lexical richness and the dynamic interactions among lexical indices in writings ( n = 150) produced by 15 Cambodian-speaking CSL learners over a school year. The results are as follows: (i) The development of CSL lexical richness is a nonlinear and fluctuating process, which fully reflects the dynamicity and complexity of lexical development. (ii) There are potential interactions among the internal indices of lexical richness. Specifically, there is a supportive interaction between lexical variation and lexical sophistication, while the lexical error rate exhibits competitive interactions with both lexical variation and lexical sophistication. (iii) Under the same learning environment, there are still obvious individual differences in the development of lexical richness. The above findings indicate that the development of lexical richness in CSL writings is a nonlinear process characterized by evident dynamicity and complexity, which requires researchers to break away from the static analytical paradigm and reexamine the entire process of Chinese lexical acquisition.

title: Female academics under the lens: emerging topics, gaps, and agenda ahead
abstract: Abstract Research on female academics has grown considerably in recent years, driven by increasing interest in gender equity within academia and the evolving challenges faced by females in this field. Despite the growing body of literature, there remains a need for a systematic analysis to map current trends, emerging topics, and underexplored areas. This study employs scientometric methods and text mining techniques to investigate the knowledge production chain in research on female academics, offering a structured overview and a future research agenda. Results reveal the dynamic evolution of knowledge production in the field, which is emerging as a systematic and interdisciplinary area of study. The analysis identifies both traditional and emerging topics, including female’s representation, recognition, and challenges, gender differences and career development, work–life balance and wellbeing, and the impact of intersectionality and multicultural contexts on female’s academic experiences. Furthermore, an examination of knowledge production and impact dissemination at national and individual levels reveals structural patterns such as center–periphery dynamics and gendered divisions of labor in academic research. These findings underscore the need to enhance international collaboration and promote gender diversity in academic research. Given the increasing emphasis on gender equity in higher education institutions worldwide, this study contributes to ongoing efforts to inform gender-sensitive policies and practices within academia.

title: Enhancing FinTech engineering education through knowledge graph integration in higher education
abstract: How can we enhance the education of financial technology (FinTech) data engineers to meet the evolving demands of engineering roles in the Greater Bay Area? This study proposes a virtual-physical integration model based on the engineering knowledge graph (KG). The model integrates virtual simulation-based teaching with real-world engineering practices in industry and development by leveraging KGs. This approach aims to elevate learners’ theoretical understanding, practical experience, and comprehensive engineering capabilities to align with the emerging requirements of the industry. The study begins by highlighting the significance, advantages, and potential applications of engineering knowledge graphs in education by analyzing the research background, objectives, and implications. It then details the theoretical framework, principles, and design components underlying the virtual-physical integration model. Using this model, learners engage in simulation-based training and hands-on problem-solving in hybrid environments, guided by KGs. A quantitative evaluation demonstrates how this approach effectively bridges the gap between educational outcomes and industry expectations, optimizing engineering capabilities. Finally, the paper discusses the strengths and limitations of the model and outlines prospects for future research, aiming to serve as a practical framework for cultivating exceptional FinTech data engineering talent.

title: An empirical analysis of the uncanny valley of human-like robots through a choice experiment in Korea
abstract: As humanoid robots and artificial intelligence technologies advance, people’s concerns about non-human entities becoming like or replacing humans are increasing. However, considering the prospect of coexistence with robots in the near future, helping people naturally adapt to this new relationship has become important. We estimated people’s utility function over social robots’ appearance, decision-making ability, voice, naturalness of motion, and emotion perception and reaction through a choice experiment. The results revealed the existence of a saddle point in people’s utility—known as the uncanny valley—as social robots’ appearance becomes more human-like. Regarding decision-making ability, people’s preference decreased as the decision autonomy of human-faced social robots increased. Our findings indicate that simply mimicking humans is insufficient for social robots to be embraced as new members of society, highlighting the need for more comprehensive considerations in their development.

title: State-owned enterprises governance architecture redesign and audit report lags: the state-owned capital authorized operation system reform in emerging markets
abstract: Audit report lags critically affect the quality of firms’ information disclosure and the effectiveness of investors’ decision-making. Using data from state-owned listed firms in China’s A-share market, the study investigates the impact of the state-owned capital authorized operation system reform (SCAOR) on audit report lags in state-owned enterprises (SOEs). The findings indicate that the SCAOR significantly reduces audit report lags in SOEs. Furthermore, the reduction effect is achieved primarily by alleviating policy burdens and enhancing internal control quality. Additional analysis shows that the relationship between the SCAOR and audit report lags is moderated by the degree of functional transformation of state-owned capital regulatory agencies, the functional types and formation modes of state-owned capital investment and operation companies, heterogeneous shareholder governance, auditor industry expertise, industry competition and regional marketization. These findings carry significant policy implications for advancing the reform of state-owned capital and SOEs, promoting the high-quality development of capital markets.

title: How digital technologies enhance firm-level energy efficiency in global climate governance
abstract: Enhancing energy efficiency is central to global climate governance, yet the role of digital technologies in this process is not fully understood. This study investigates the effects of artificial intelligence, blockchain, cloud computing, and big data on firm-level energy efficiency. Drawing on panel data from 2003 Chinese A-share listed companies between 2013 and 2021, we employ the method of moments quantile regression to capture heterogeneous impacts across efficiency levels. The findings show that digital technologies significantly improve energy efficiency across all quantiles (10th–90th), with the most substantial improvements occurring among the least efficient firms (10th quantile). An energy rebound effect is also observed. Moreover, a composite index of digital technologies consistently outperforms individual technologies in promoting efficiency gains. These results highlight the potential of digital innovation to enhance corporate sustainability and provide policy guidance for advancing the global energy transition.

title: Role of government and information trust in public perception of environmental risk: a case study of treated contaminated water discharge in Fukushima
abstract: Despite growing public concern regarding the marine discharge of Fukushima treated contaminated water (FTCW), trust aspects related to risk perception remain underexplored. We used a nationally representative survey in South Korea to investigate the independent and interactive associations of government and information trust with cognitive and affective dimensions of risk perception regarding FTCW. Increased government trust was associated with lower perceived risk, consistent with the “paradox of trust” theory. Information trust functioned as a conditional factor, where the association between government trust and risk perception was notably attenuated among those who viewed information as non-exaggerated. Risk perception was notably higher among women, low-income groups, and primary industry workers, reflecting socioeconomic vulnerability. This study advances theoretical understanding by highlighting that information appraisal conditions institutional trust dynamics, challenging traditional information deficit models. Practically, it underscores the need for context-congruent communication and sequencing to foster public support for nuclear-related policy.

title: Coupling mechanisms between ecosystem services and sustainable development in old revolutionary base areas of Jiangxi, Fujian, and Guangdong, China
abstract: Abstract Balancing ecosystem conservation and sustainable development remains a fundamental governance challenge in policy-intensive and ecologically sensitive regions. As a convergence zone of red cultural heritage, poverty-alleviation policies, and a critical ecological barrier in southern China, the old revolutionary areas in Jiangxi, Fujian, and Guangdong (JFG-ROBAs) provide a policy-relevant case for examining interactions between ecosystem services (ESs) and sustainable development (SD) under strong administrative intervention and uneven regional development. This study aims to clarify the scale-conditional and service-specific coupling mechanisms between ESs and SD in JFG-ROBAs and to derive implications for trajectory-aware sustainability governance. Using data from 2001 to 2022, we conduct a comparative analysis between the province-wide city context (41 cities, grouped by province) and the policy-area (JFG-ROBAs) city scale (17 cities). Sustainable development is assessed through an entropy-weighted multi-dimensional indicator system, while four ecosystem services—Habitat quality (HQ), Carbon storage (CS), Soil retention (SR), and Water yield (WY)—are quantified using the InVEST model. Interactions between sustainable development and ecosystem services (SDESs) are examined using coupling coordination degree (CCD) analysis and spatiotemporal correlation tests. The results indicate that ecosystem services in JFG-ROBAs have undergone systematic deterioration over time. Habitat quality continues to decline, carbon storage recovery is volatile, and both soil retention and water yield decrease markedly after historical peaks. Across all dimensions of sustainable development, the policy-area (JFG-ROBAs) city scale consistently lags behind the province-wide city context, with the largest gap observed in Sustainability acceleration, reflecting persistent constraints in education and employment capacity. Interprovincial comparisons further reveal pronounced structural disparities, indicating that strong development performance at the provincial level does not necessarily translate into equivalent progress within designated policy areas. More importantly, spatiotemporal SDES analyses reveal a distinct “statistical synergy–substantive conflict” pattern. While cross-sectional correlations suggest weak positive alignment or apparent coordination between ecosystem services and sustainable development, longitudinal trajectories demonstrate cumulative ecological degradation accompanying development expansion. This divergence indicates that static coordination assessments can mask long-term ecological costs embedded in development pathways. These findings underscore the necessity of trajectory-aware and service-specific governance strategies that move beyond static coordination metrics, offering transferable insights for managing sustainability trade-offs in ecologically constrained, policy-driven regions.

title: Evolution of ecosystem service values and their drivers in the ESG era: evidence from China
abstract: Understanding the evolution of ecosystem service value (ESV) is crucial for promoting sustainable development and aligning environmental management with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles. This study investigates the spatial–temporal dynamics of ESV across China and explores its key driving factors in the context of the emerging ESG era. In this study, a comprehensive input–output evaluation system was constructed to measure the ESV conversion efficiency of 31 provinces (autonomous regions and municipalities) in China from 2000 to 2022 using the Super-SBM model. Spatial statistical analysis was then conducted to examine the spatiotemporal patterns of ESV conversion efficiency across multiple scales, and the driving factors were identified with the aid of the GeoDetector model. The results indicate that: (1) China’s ESV conversion efficiency exhibits a significant positive spatial correlation overall, with evident local H–H (high–high) and L–L (low–low) clustering characteristics. (2) The spatiotemporal distribution of ESV conversion efficiency presents a pronounced scale effect. At the national level, the efficiency’s center of gravity shows a westward shift, demonstrating the overall pattern of being strong in the east and weak in the west. Regionally, eastern China maintains the highest efficiency, while western China displays a clear downward trend. At the provincial level, Guangdong and Shanghai rank among the most efficient, whereas Gansu, Ningxia, and Qinghai remain at the lower end. (3) Environmental attention and the level of marketization are identified as key determinants of ESV conversion efficiency. Moreover, the interaction between environmental attention and openness, as well as that between marketization and environmental attention, was the primary combined forces explaining the spatial variation in efficiency. The findings highlight the need to integrate ESG-driven governance mechanisms into ecosystem management and regional development planning, thereby providing policy insights for balancing ecological value enhancement with sustainable economic growth in China.

title: Graduate students’ career aspirations: insights into influencing factors and expectations
abstract: Career decision-making represents a critical transition point for graduate students, particularly in contexts where misalignment between higher education outcomes and labor market opportunities persists. Despite increasing concerns regarding graduate employability, limited empirical research has examined how multiple factors jointly shape graduate students’ career aspirations, especially in developing countries. This study addresses this gap by investigating the determinants influencing graduate students’ preferences for academic versus non-academic career pathways. The study draws on cross-sectional survey data collected from 464 final-year graduate students enrolled in public and private universities. A binary logistic regression model is employed to examine the influence of individual characteristics, family background, training experiences, academic discipline, and job related attributes on career choice. The findings indicate that a slight majority of graduate students express a preference for academic careers at the final stage of their studies, although career expectations evolve over time. Intrinsic motivation, supervisory support, and perceived opportunities for career development emerge as significant factors increasing the likelihood of choosing academic careers. In contrast, higher income expectations are associated with a stronger inclination toward non-academic career pathways. The results further reveal observable differences across gender and academic disciplines in shaping career preferences. These findings underline the importance of strengthening institutional support mechanisms, particularly mentorship and career guidance, to facilitate informed career decision-making. The study contributes to a deeper understanding of career development processes in higher education and highlights the need to better align graduate outcomes with evolving labor market demands.

title: Empowering through participation: how effective participation influences farmers’ rights and interests in rural homestead withdrawal in China
abstract: Abstract Although withdrawal from rural homesteads (WRH) focus on farmers’ rights and interests, a gap between policy commitments and implementation persists due to ineffective participation. Furthermore, existing literature has yet to effectively unpack the “black box” of how participation translates into the protection of farmers’ rights and interests. To address this, this study constructs an integrative analytical framework of effective participation influencing farmers’ rights and interests. Farmers’ rights and interests are operationalized into three dimensions (living, economic, and social). Also, the framework innovatively incorporates participation awareness as a core element of effective participation. The proposed framework is empirically examined using micro-level survey data from Sichuan Province. The results show that: (1) Farmers’ effective participation is an important factor in protecting their rights in the WRH. (2) Farmers’ effective participation significantly prioritizes living right, followed by economic right, with minimal effect on social right in the process of WRH. (3) Participation awareness has the greatest influence among all elements, acting as the primary starting point for improvement of rights and interests. Participation outcomes, participation ability, and participation support follow in importance. (4) Effective participation may also widen disparities, as its positive impact increases with higher levels of these rights and interests. These findings indicate that improving the mechanism of farmers’ participation, enhancing their participation ability, and motivating them to participate can protect farmers’ rights and interests. Also, local governments should focus on the disparity of rights and interests with targeted measures to address them.

title: To what extent do GPT language models capture human sentence processing dynamics? Evidence from Korean subject honorification
abstract: The present study investigates how GPT language models approximate human sentence-processing dynamics in Korean subject honorification. Drawing upon four open-access datasets from prior psycholinguistic experiments—acceptability judgements, politeness ratings, self-paced reading, and eye-tracking reading—we compare human performance with surprisal estimates from three Korean-capable GPT variants (KoGPT-2, Ko-GPT-Trinity, and mGPT). Across tasks, the models reliably detect coarse morphosyntactic violations, assigning high surprisal to clear honorific-agreement mismatches that elicit low acceptability and processing slowdowns in humans. However, GPT surprisal fails to capture graded, context-dependent aspects of behaviour, including the optionality of the subject honorific suffix, animacy-sensitive politeness judgements, and delayed spillover effects in reading. Correlations between human measures and model surprisal are consistently weak and highly condition-specific. These findings suggest that GPT language models provide a useful but limited proxy for human sentence processing: they track whether inputs are broadly well-formed but underrepresent the socio-pragmatic and discourse-level constraints that shape processing dynamics in Korean. This calls for more cognitively and culturally appropriate approaches to computational metrics for explainable AI in language sciences.

title: From CEO to innovator: how entrepreneurial orientation relates to employee innovation across organizational levels
abstract: Employee innovation is a key driver of organizational renewal and long-term competitiveness, yet less is known about how CEO-level entrepreneurial orientations are associated with employees’ innovative behavior across organizational levels. Drawing on the attention-based view, this study examines whether CEO entrepreneurial orientation (CEO EO) is associated with employee innovative behavior through a senior-executive-rated innovation-oriented cultural orientation, and whether this cultural pathway depends on environmental dynamism and competitiveness (EDC). Using matched multilevel data from 149 Chinese firms, 554 departments, and 2540 employees, this study finds that CEO EO is positively associated with employee innovative behavior and that this association is mediated by senior-executive-rated innovation-oriented cultural orientation. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that EDC weakens the association between CEO EO and senior-executive-rated innovation-oriented cultural orientation, suggesting that turbulent and competitive environments may disrupt the consistency and institutionalization through which CEO EO is translated into innovation-oriented cultural signals. The conditional indirect-effect results further indicate that the indirect association between CEO EO and employee innovative behavior through senior-executive-rated innovation-oriented cultural orientation is stronger when EDC is lower rather than higher. These findings extend CEO EO research by linking CEO-level entrepreneurial orientation to employee-level innovation, clarify one organizational-level cultural pathway, and identify a boundary condition under which entrepreneurial leadership signals are less consistently translated into innovation-oriented cultural orientations.

title: Ant colony intelligence optimization of asset portfolios under constraints—dynamic risk adjustment and Sharpe ratio maximization
abstract: Abstract This study addresses the challenge of constrained portfolio optimization by proposing a novel framework based on an enhanced Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm. Building upon the Markowitz mean-variance foundation, we propose a hybrid framework that integrates Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) for discrete asset selection under cardinality constraints with quadratic programming for optimal weight allocation subject to no-short-selling and budget constraints. Dynamic risk estimation is achieved by employing EWMA and GARCH(1,1) models on rolling windows to update the covariance matrix during optimization. The latter is achieved by employing EWMA and GARCH(1,1) models on rolling windows to update the covariance matrix during optimization. We introduce key enhancements to the ACO algorithm, such as an elite retention strategy and an adaptive pheromone update mechanism linked to asset weights, to improve convergence and solution quality under complex constraints. Empirical validation is conducted using historical daily returns from a stratified sample of 20 S&P 500 stocks. Results demonstrate that the enhanced ACO significantly outperforms benchmark algorithms (PSO and GA), yielding portfolios with higher Sharpe ratios (average improvement of 10–15% on test set) and superior risk control (reduced maximum drawdown by 5–7%). Robust performance is maintained across both bull and bear market regimes. This research provides an effective heuristic optimization approach for quantitative multi-factor strategy design, offering practical value for real-world asset allocation under constraints.

title: More teaching, less promotion: analysing the relationship between female faculty’s teaching commitment and academic promotion in China
abstract: Women account for a larger share of university faculty in China than in many developed countries, yet limited research has examined gender differences in teaching commitment and whether its association with academic promotion varies by gender. Drawing on nationally representative data from the 2017 China University Faculty Survey, covering 2366 faculty members across 30 universities, we use survival analysis to assess how teaching commitment, measured by time devoted to teaching, relates to the timing of academic promotion and whether this association differs by gender. We find that female faculty report significantly higher teaching commitment than male colleagues. However, higher teaching commitment is associated with slower promotion overall, and this negative association is more pronounced for women. By providing large-scale evidence from a non-Western context where teaching has been explicitly prioritised in promotion reforms, this study informs cross-national debates on academic careers and gender equity and suggests that formal criteria reforms may be insufficient to ensure equitable faculty advancement.

title: Impact mechanisms and policy regulation of human socioeconomic activities on mangrove evolution in China’s coastal cities
abstract: In recent years, the spatial dynamics of mangrove ecosystems in China have exhibited a complex pattern of both restoration and degradation, reflecting the multifaceted and spatiotemporally heterogeneous impacts of human activities, yet these dynamics remain insufficiently understood. This study employs city-level panel data from 2003 to 2023 to investigate how coastal urban activities influence mangrove ecosystems across four dimensions: socioeconomic pressure, marine industrial development, pollution load and environmental governance, and ecosystem status. Using fixed effects models, spatiotemporal heterogeneity models, and moderation models, we identify the evolving impact mechanisms of urban coastal activities on mangroves, with particular attention to the moderating role of environmental protection investment. The empirical results reveal that industrial pollution and habitat fragmentation significantly suppress mangrove area. However, environmental protection investment plays a crucial moderating role in mitigating the negative impacts of marine industrial expansion, highlighting the irreplaceability of environmental governance to foster ecological–economic synergies. Regionally, the Pearl River Delta exhibits a pronounced negative effect from marine economic activities, whereas Guangxi demonstrates a strong moderating influence from environmental investment, resulting in an overall positive impact of urban activity factors. These findings offer robust empirical support for enhancing environmental governance and industrial restructuring in coastal cities, and provide theoretical and policy insights for developing resilience-oriented sustainable development strategies.

title: Why an artificial agent may change the given final goal
abstract: The debate about the possible future creation of superhuman artificial agents is characterized by an extreme contrast of positions: Some thinkers expect that such agents will enable us to overcome poverty, disease, and even death. Others fear that they will cause the extinction of our species. Curiously, both positions rest on the same assumption, namely, that an artificial agent will never change the given final goal. Against this assumption, the present paper shows that an agent operating in the real world will face the problem that the given goal is inevitably ambiguous to some extent. To resolve this ambiguity, the agent will have to acquire an understanding of the reason(s) that underlie the goal. And a consequence of this understanding may be that the agent then changes the goal. The upshot of the paper is that superhuman artificial agents will be neither our obedient servants nor blind engines of destruction. Rather, they will be responsive to the reasons that they encounter as they come to understand the world.

title: Climate risk and corporate greenwashing: evidence from China
abstract: This study provides a systematic examination of how climate risk exposure influences corporate greenwashing, addressing a critical gap in understanding mechanisms connecting climate policy uncertainty to opportunistic environmental disclosure. Using panel data covering 1358 Chinese listed firms from 2009 to 2023, we measure firm-level climate risk exposure through stock return sensitivity to China’s Climate Policy Uncertainty index and operationalize greenwashing as the divergence between Bloomberg’s ESG disclosure scores and Huazheng’s ESG performance ratings. Drawing on the fraud triangle framework, we argue that climate risk simultaneously creates pressure (stakeholder demands amid resource constraints), opportunity (discretionary disclosure with limited verification), and rationalization (wait-and-see justifications) that incentivize symbolic over substantive environmental responses. Employing fixed effects panel regressions with instrumental variable analysis using Bartik-style shift-share instruments, we document that a one-standard-deviation increase in climate risk exposure increases greenwashing by 0.15 standard deviations. This relationship is amplified by managerial power and short-termism but attenuated by strong internal controls and independent analyst coverage. State-owned enterprises and heavy polluters demonstrate particularly strong sensitivities, reflecting regulatory catering dynamics. Our findings contribute to the growing literature on climate risk and corporate behavior by demonstrating that climate risk exposure incentivizes symbolic rather than substantive environmental compliance.

title: Network-driven DDPG for low-risk energy portfolios
abstract: Under the dual challenges of global warming and environmental degradation, the global demand for energy continues to escalate, accompanied by an increasing emphasis on technological innovation. The new energy sector has emerged as a pivotal driver for sustainable development. This study investigates China’s new energy industry through the integration of complex network theory and deep reinforcement learning models. By synergizing complex network analysis with the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm, we quantitatively examine risk interdependencies and node significance among listed enterprises using statistical metrics, ultimately aiming to achieve portfolio risk diversification and return enhancement. A multi-layer complex network model is constructed to analyze risk correlations within the new energy sector. A composite evaluation index is developed to identify low-centrality stocks, forming a stock pool characterized by reduced risk interconnectedness. The DDPG algorithm is then applied to optimize portfolio allocation strategies, balancing risk diversification with the dual objectives of maximizing returns and minimizing volatility. In conclusion, this research demonstrates that complex networks can quantitatively describe the degree of interconnection among assets in the new energy sector. By comparing low-centrality portfolios with full-sample portfolios, the study shows that low-centrality strategies combined with the DDPG model perform better in terms of risk control and returns. Furthermore, the comprehensive centrality index evaluation can identify marginally traded stocks with differentiated risk profiles, thereby providing investors in the new energy sector with a scientifically sound and reasonable portfolio strategy.

title: Exploring the sustainable development of regional culture by tourist souvenir design—development and application of Pingyao lacquerware tourism souvenir model
abstract: Despite the rapid growth of cultural tourism making souvenirs an increasingly important medium for disseminating regional culture, Pingyao lacquerware souvenirs generally lack distinct regional characteristics and insufficient cultural expression. The primary reason is the scarcity of professional designers in this field, with production relying on craftsmen who lack systematic training. This study aims to develop a souvenir model that helps practitioners balance cultural expression and design guidance by introducing a Pingyao regional culture module based on the CFBSS model. Through semi-structured interviews, the research systematically identified 6 dimensions and 19 sub-dimensions of Pingyao’s regional culture. Based on encoding-decoding theory, a three-layer regional cultural structure—macro, meso, and micro—was constructed to refine the original model. Subsequently, six experts validated the new model, and the results confirmed its effectiveness. The developed model not only provides systematic guidance for designers and craftsmen in the lacquerware field during the design process, promoting the effective expression of local cultural elements, but also provides a reference for the development of other intangible cultural heritage tourism souvenirs.

title: A post-structuralist analysis of sustainability as a new hegemonic identity
abstract: Abstract Sustainability has become a central concept in global policy agendas, corporate strategies, and civil society discourse. Yet, despite its ubiquity, the term often functions as a vague ideal, encompassing divergent-and at times conflicting-interests. This study addresses the critical gap in understanding how sustainability operates not merely as an environmental or developmental goal, but as a discursive construction that shapes political identities and power relations. Drawing on post-structuralist theory, particularly the works of Foucault, Derrida, Laclau, and Mouffe, the research investigates how sustainability functions as a hegemonic identity by marginalizing alternative narratives and securing broad ideological consensus. Employing critical discourse analysis, the study examines policy documents and public narratives from the European Union, the United Nations, and Turkey to trace how sustainability is articulated, institutionalized, and contested in different governance settings. The findings indicate that sustainability has evolved into an “empty signifier”-a flexible concept that unites diverse agendas under a common rhetorical umbrella. While this discursive openness facilitates global alignment, it also allows for co-optation, symbolic politics, and the suppression of transformative alternatives. Emerging critiques such as degrowth and climate justice movements reveal the fragility of this consensus and highlight growing resistance to technocratic and market-driven sustainability models. By situating sustainability within a broader field of ideological struggle, the study underscores its unstable and contested nature. Recognizing the discursive mechanisms that elevate sustainability to hegemonic status opens space for more pluralistic, democratic, and justice-oriented sustainability imaginaries. These insights carry important implications for rethinking policy frameworks and grassroots strategies in the face of ecological and political crises.

title: How can outpatient pooling reform alleviate health inequalities: evidence from China’s basic medical insurance
abstract: While some studies find that the outpatient pooling reform (OPR) of Chinese basic medical insurance can improve the service utilization of participants and alleviate health inequalities within the system, no research has focused on its effect on the inequality among different systems. Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, this study measured the inequalities existing in healthcare service utilization and health outcomes between two groups of participants in the Urban Employee Basic Medical Insurance (UEBMI) and Urban and Rural Resident Basic Medical Insurance (URRBMI), and estimated how the OPR can alleviate the inequalities using the Staggered Difference-in-Difference method. The results show that the OPR had a significant alleviating effect on the narrowed fairness gaps faced by resident participants from 2011 to 2020, with the effect varying with the reform sequences in the two insurances. The reforms implemented simultaneously in the two insurances narrowed the disadvantage of residents in health outcomes, but widened the gap in their service utilization. In regions where the reform was first implemented in UEBMI, the later reform in URRBMI narrowed the gap in service utilization but widened the gap in health outcomes. In areas where the reform was first implemented in URRBMI, the gaps faced by residents did not change significantly after the implementation of OPR in UEBMI. Mechanism analysis indicates that the narrowing inequality was partly caused by the ex-post moral hazard of employee participants, the ex-ante moral hazard of resident participants, and the adverse selection of the two types of participants.

title: Why skills alone are not enough: belonging, recognition, and youth livelihoods in rural India
abstract: Belonging is often treated in development policy as a secondary, affective outcome of economic participation. This study challenges that assumption by arguing that belonging operates as a structuring condition that precedes and shapes recognition, rather than emerging as a by-product of participation. Focusing on rural India, where informal labour, caste hierarchies, and limited institutional access intersect, it examines how the marginalization of belonging within skill development frameworks reproduces social and economic exclusion. Drawing on qualitative evidence from two focus group discussions (FGDs) with forty-one rural youth and three key informants in Moti-Borvai, Gujarat, the study analyses how caste, gender, and informal skills shape pathways into work and conditions of social legitimacy. The findings indicate that exclusion operates at both material and symbolic levels. Caste functions as an often-unspoken boundary shaping access to employment, while gendered norms restrict women’s mobility and frame belonging in terms of domestic roles. At the same time, locally acquired informal skills are systematically devalued within institutional systems that privilege formal credentials, producing competence without recognition. In response, the study develops the Belonging-Recognition-Justice (BRJ) Framework, which conceptualizes livelihood inclusion through alignment between social legitimacy, institutional recognition, and redistributive justice.
