This framework offers an empirically grounded approach that explains exclusion even where skills are present, addressing a key limitation in dominant skill-based frameworks, with implications for inclusive development in rural India and across the Global South.

title: Correction: Towards a deeper understanding of information manipulation: Proposing a multilevel framework for the analysis of manipulative narratives
abstract: Correction to: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06656-8 , published online 06 February 2026

title: How parental lying relates to disordered eating
abstract: Parental lying is a frequently used parenting strategy that has been linked to psychosocial outcomes, yet its association with disordered eating remains uncertain. Moreover, the role of perceived maternal psychological control and internalizing symptoms in this context has yet to be examined. 302 adults ( M age = 27, 83% female) completed validated self-report measures of retrospectively reported parental lying, perceived maternal psychological control, internalizing symptoms, and disordered eating. Path analysis examined indirect associations through perceived maternal psychological control and internalizing symptoms, controlling for gender, age, education, income, employment status, and BMI. Results showed that retrospectively reported parental lying was not significantly related to internalizing symptoms ( β = 0.08, p = 0.166) or directly to disordered eating ( β = 0.05, p = 0.399). The indirect association through higher perceived maternal psychological control and internalizing symptoms was significant ( β = 0.02, p = 0.011), while the effects through internalizing symptoms alone ( β = 0.02, p = 0.207) and perceived control alone ( β = 0.05, p = 0.077) were not significant. Retrospectively reported parental lying was not directly associated with disordered eating or internalizing symptoms; only the full sequential indirect estimate, through higher perceived maternal psychological control and internalizing symptoms, was statistically significant. The findings are best interpreted as hypothesis-generating, specifying a theoretically constrained sequence that can be tested or revised in prospective, multi-informant research rather than establishing a confirmed mechanism.

title: Balancing language and design: analyzing university teaching practices in CLIL contexts through the UTBO-CLIL framework
abstract: This study examines how university instructors balance disciplinary content and language development in CLIL art and design courses in higher education. Drawing on the adapted University Teaching Behaviour Observation-Content and Language Integrated Learning (UTBO-CLIL) framework, it analyzes 1080 min of virtual classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, and weekly reflective journals from 10 instructors and 60 undergraduate students in CLIL-integrated design courses in Zhejiang, China. The study asks how instructors’ observable behaviours align with UTBO-CLIL categories and what challenges shape the use of non-directive pedagogy. The findings show that directive behaviours, including giving directions, demonstrating techniques and providing information, were more frequent than non-directive behaviours, especially during technically complex or time-constrained tasks. Non-directive moves such as open questioning, scaffolding and offering choice were present, but they tended to occur episodically rather than as a consistently planned feature of lesson design. Interview and journal data suggest that instructors’ reliance on directive strategies was shaped by time pressure, limited CLIL-specific training and uncertainty about how to integrate design discourse with language support. Cultural and semiotic diversity also influenced classroom interaction, particularly when students drew on locally embedded design meanings that were not always fully recognized in assessment or feedback. The study suggests that UTBO-CLIL can provide a useful observational lens for identifying tensions between pedagogical intentions and classroom practices in creative CLIL settings. It also points to the need for discipline-specific teacher development that supports language-sensitive, culturally responsive and multimodal forms of studio pedagogy.

title: Modeling competing narratives in adaptive networks: how social pressure and network dynamics drive tipping and persistence
abstract: Contested narratives on social media often spread in bursts: most remain localized, yet a few tip into rapid diffusion and reshape polarized network structure. We develop an agent-based model of competing narrative diffusion on an adaptive network to explain when such tipping dynamics occur. In the model, sharing produces social feedback that reinforces conviction, adoption is modulated by time-varying collective attention, and ties coevolve as agents rewire based on disagreement. We also include committed seeders ("zealots”) to represent persistent promotion. Across simulation experiments, we identify two recurring diffusion pathways. Under strong social pressure and highly adaptive networks, diffusion exhibits rapid, localized bursts that consolidate ideologically homogeneous clusters-accelerating tipping while restricting cross-group reach. Under more moderate network adaptation, diffusion proceeds more gradually yet reaches a broader portion of the network through bridging ties, producing wider reach with less extreme segregation. Attention decay creates a finite window for large-scale diffusion; nonetheless, once established within polarized clusters, diffusion can persist at a nontrivial level even as attention wanes when zealots continue seeding. Finally, asymmetric zealot deployment across groups generates divergent outcomes, with one group consolidating into a more homogeneous cluster while the other becomes larger but more internally heterogeneous. The model offers a general mechanism for bursty narrative diffusion in coevolving networks, with implications for disinformation campaigns serving as an application context where strategic seeding and identity-consistent reinforcement may be especially salient.

title: Mapping cybersecurity literacy: inequality, capability, and digital vulnerability in India
abstract: Abstract Cybersecurity literacy has become a global concern as digital infrastructures expand rapidly, exposing populations to risks associated with fraud, misinformation, and data exploitation. Yet empirical evidence on how cybersecurity literacy remains sparse. This study examines India, one of the world’s largest and fastest-digitising societies, to assess the extent and social stratification of cybersecurity literacy. Using nationally representative data from the 79th Round of the National Sample Survey (July 2022 to June 2023), encompassing 9,70,934 individuals, the analysis maps cybersecurity skills across caste, gender, education, age, income, and region. The findings reveal extremely low levels of cybersecurity literacy nationwide, with only 15.7 percent of adults able to perform basic digital security tasks. These deficits are unevenly distributed, with rural women from Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities exhibiting the lowest levels of security capability. Framed through the Capability Approach and second-level digital divide perspectives, the results show that expanding digital access does not guarantee secure or equitable participation. Without targeted interventions that address structural inequalities, digital transformation risks entrenching existing forms of inequality and creating new layers of digital insecurity.

title: Do environmental taxes improve environmental sustainability beyond net-zero emissions? Evidence from ecological footprint subcomponents in the EU
abstract: Abstract Environmental degradation has manifested in various forms, including air and water pollution. Therefore, the impacts of environmental policies should be evaluated across all dimensions of environmental degradation. The European Union has targeted to stop CO 2 emissions by 2050. Accordingly, the literature has predominantly focused on the relationship between environmental taxation and CO₂ emissions. Even if the net-zero emissions target is achieved, this does not necessarily ensure the elimination of overall environmental degradation. This study investigates the impact of environmental taxation on environmental degradation in the European Union over the period 1995–2021 using the Driscoll-Kraay (1998) estimator. The study focuses on the impact of environmental tax on ecological footprint and its subcomponents. The findings show that the ecological footprint and its subcomponents, except for built-up land and forest product footprints, can be mitigated by current environmental tax policies. However, in order to achieve net-zero environmental degradation, the European Union must reduce pressures arising from built-up land and forest product footprints. In addition to the Driscoll-Kraay (1998) estimator, the Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) estimator is employed as a robustness check, and the results remain broadly consistent across both methods. Moreover, Dumitrescu and Hurlin (2012) causality test states that strong and bidirectional causal relationships between environmental tax and ecological footprint components. This overall result confirms the existence of a green dividend within the double dividend hypothesis. It is suggested that renewable energy plants should be constructed in areas where built-up land and forest products footprint are not affected. For example, floating solar panels do not use land and also protect water bodies from evaporation.

title: Are confidence in self and the healthcare system plausible pathways linking chronic conditions to subjective health and wellbeing?
abstract: Abstract Chronic conditions are known to reduce subjective wellbeing (SWB) and self-rated health (SRH), yet the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly understood. Using nationally representative Australian data (2011: N = 1946; 2021: N = 1050), we examined whether psychological self-confidence (SC) and confidence in the healthcare system (HSC) are associated with these outcomes above and beyond chronic condition status, drawing on Weems’ Associational Variable Analysis framework. Chronic condition status was significantly and negatively associated with SRH (2011: β = –0.826; 2021: B = –0.597) and SWB (2011: β = –0.371; 2021: β = –0.250). SC positively associated with both SRH (2011: β = 0.239; 2021: β = 0.287) and SWB (2011: β = 0.584; 2021: β = 0.570), explaining a substantial share of variance in these outcomes beyond chronic condition status (SRH: 11–14%; SWB: 63–64%). HSC contributed smaller but significant associations with both outcomes. These patterns were broadly consistent across both survey waves. Although temporal ordering and causality cannot be established due to the cross-sectional nature of the data, the results generate the hypotheses that both SC and HSC may help explain the association between chronic condition status and SRH and SWB in Australia, a proposition that awaits testing with longitudinal data and appropriate causal designs.

title: Fairness evaluation of large language models in academic library reference services
abstract: Abstract As libraries explore large language models (LLMs) for use in virtual reference services, a key question arises: Can LLMs serve all users equitably, regardless of demographics or social status? While they offer great potential for scalable support, LLMs may also reproduce societal biases embedded in their training data, risking the integrity of libraries’ commitment to equitable service. To address this concern, we evaluate whether LLMs differentiate responses across user identities by prompting six state-of-the-art LLMs to assist patrons differing in sex, race/ethnicity, and institutional role. We find no evidence of differentiation by race or ethnicity, and only minor evidence of stereotypical bias against women in one model. LLMs demonstrate nuanced accommodation of institutional roles through the use of linguistic choices related to formality, politeness, and domain-specific vocabularies, reflecting professional norms rather than discriminatory treatment. These findings suggest that current LLMs show a promising degree of readiness to support equitable and contextually appropriate communication in academic library reference services.

title: From disciplines to concepts: beyond (inter-)disciplinarity in legal knowledge generation
abstract: Abstract Law is both a ubiquitous social phenomenon and an academic discipline. However, unlike with knowledge generated in many other disciplines, legal knowledge has come to sit uneasily with the notions of science. The 20 th century saw increased alienation between law and science. On the one hand, doctrinal approaches separate “legal science” from other domains of knowledge but struggle to be accepted as scientific by the broader scientific community. On the other hand, calls for infusing perspectives and methods from other disciplines into law raise questions on whether anything distinct remains in such interdisciplinary legal scholarship as opposed to its merging with other academic disciplines. The genealogy of dominant ways of legal knowledge generation as the process of creating authoritative research results that sustain and enhance the legitimacy of law as a discipline demonstrates this alienation amidst growing emphasis on “interdisciplinary” scholarship, and prompts the question of how the alienation may be remedied. This article argues that interdisciplinarity is an overly limited logic and advocates an alternative logic beyond disciplines that begins with key overarching political concepts, more than with merely interdisciplinary engagement. Legal knowledge is particularly suitable to be welcoming towards such a shift due to its interest in concepts and linkages to legal practice that underscore its practical relevance. The article argues that the study of concepts allows for a less dominating—and hence more democratic—engagement beyond disciplines, because it does not require rigid disciplinary identities. Although the focus on concepts cannot altogether replace working within disciplines, the findings point to the potential of more diverse academic spaces, often found in the “Global South”, to contribute to democratizing legal knowledge generation thanks to the relatively weaker straitjacket of disciplinary separation in general and alienation between law and science in particular in these spaces.

title: Possible future outlook for sustainable higher education amidst demographic decline: modelling university population trends in Slovakia for the year 2040
abstract: Demographic changes, particularly long-term shifts and fluctuations in the size and age structure of potential student cohorts, pose significant challenges for universities. The declining numbers directly impact enrolment levels, funding mechanisms, and the long-term sustainability of higher education systems. Understanding demographic trends is crucial for strategic planning and adapting to changing patterns of student participation. In response to concerning demographic statistics and forecasts, this study explores the future trajectory of the Slovak university population up to 2040, employing two complementary projection models integrated with regional population forecasts. The cohort model estimates the future size of the domestic Slovak university student population by applying recent age- and sex-specific enrolment rates to projected population cohorts, while the Regional model estimates this population by applying recent region of origin enrolment rates to projected regional population cohorts. The study uses databases from the Statistical Office and the Centre of Scientific and Technical Information of the Slovak Republic. The reference period for analysing gross enrolment ratios by age and sex spans 2018–2022, while the cohort size outlook covers the years 2010–2022. Population development varies significantly across Slovak regions, with different population potentials for the higher education sector. Both models suggest a short-term decline until 2026, followed by a modest recovery, with the domestic student population increasing by ~4–6%, primarily due to the expansion of cohorts under 26. The cohort and regional models identify potential prospects for university cohorts in Slovakia and highlight the timing and scale of turnover after 2026. Incorporating demographic factors into projection models can support more timely and regionally differentiated planning responses in higher education. Understanding the declining university population in Slovakia requires a multidimensional analysis that considers not only demographic but also economic, political, and sociocultural factors. Slovak universities face challenges that require strategic responses and proactive approaches. Only in this way will they be able to adapt to changing demographic conditions while remaining relevant and competitive internationally.

title: ArchiveGPT: A human-centered evaluation of using a vision language model for image cataloguing
abstract: Abstract The accelerating growth of photographic collections has outpaced manual cataloguing, motivating the use of vision language models (VLMs) to automate metadata generation. This study examines whether AI-generated catalogue descriptions can approximate human-written quality and how generative AI might integrate into cataloguing workflows in archival and museum collections. A VLM ( InternVL2 ) generated catalogue descriptions for photographic prints on labelled cardboard mounts with archaeological content. After a human-in-the-loop curation process, they were evaluated by archive and archaeology experts (consisting of students and professionals) and non-experts in a human-centred, experimental framework. Participants classified descriptions as AI-generated or expert-written, rated quality, and reported willingness to use and trust in AI tools. Classification performance was above chance level, with both groups underestimating their ability to detect AI-generated descriptions. OCR errors and hallucinations limited perceived quality, yet descriptions rated higher in accuracy and usefulness were harder to classify. This suggests that even further human review is necessary to ensure the accuracy and quality of the catalogue descriptions generated by the out-of-the-box model and selected by humans, particularly in specialized domains like archaeological cataloguing. Experts showed lower willingness to adopt AI tools, emphasizing concerns on preservation responsibility over technical performance. These findings advocate for a collaborative approach where AI supports draft generation but remains subordinate to human verification, ensuring alignment with curatorial values (e.g., provenance, transparency). The successful integration of this approach depends on technical advancements, such as domain-specific fine-tuning, and on establishing trust among professionals. Both could be fostered through a transparent and explainable AI pipeline.

title: Online written peer feedback on speaking performance: Learner perceptions and preferences
abstract: Peer feedback, being an essential component of the learning process, was relatively ignored in terms of its connection to speaking skills, despite a vast amount of research on specifically peer feedback and feedback in general, particularly in writing. In this sense, this study aimed to examine the effect of written peer feedback on learners’ speaking performance and find out the feedback types preferred by students when providing online written peer feedback. It also sought to explore the perceptions of learners regarding online peer feedback exchange. This study followed a mixed-method approach, combining both quantitative data obtained through pre- and post-speaking tests and qualitative data through online written feedback of learners and semi-structured interviews. Twenty-nine tertiary-level students who were enrolled in a listening and speaking course participated in the study. The participants were given assignments to prepare four video presentations collaboratively as out-of-class tasks and then were asked to receive and give online written peer feedback after each video presentation in class over an academic term. Content analysis was conducted to analyze the qualitative data, and a paired samples t-test was carried out to reveal whether the speaking post-test results significantly differed from their speaking pre-test results. The results demonstrated that peer feedback significantly improved the overall speaking performance of learners, as well as their fluency, vocabulary, and pronunciation. Moreover, the participants developed positive attitudes towards peer feedback regarding pronunciation and motivation, and the expressive-approval feedback was determined to be the most preferred type for providing online written peer feedback. In conclusion, online peer feedback had both academic and affective benefits, and it should be integrated into the speaking classes considering the feedback perceptions and preferences of learners.

title: Evolving kinship networks of population-hollowing villages within rapid urbanization: the Liangshan area in China as the case
abstract: Addressing the challenges of rural revitalization in the context of rapid urbanization—including the population decline, insufficient infrastructure, and the disintegration of kinship networks of ethnic minority villages—is essential for achieving sustainable rural development. This paper studied Yubu Village, an ethnic Yi community in China’s Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, with the aim of investigating the spatiotemporal evolution and reconstruction of its kinship networks. To achieve this, 20-year in-situ data between 2003 and 2023 were collected, including occupation, population mobility, and kinship ties of Yubu Village. Kinship networks for 2003, 2009, and 2023 were then built through social network analysis (SNA), by calculating key indicators such as network density, k-core, and degree centrality. ArcMap was employed to project these network structures into geographic space, enabling analysis of the spatiotemporal evolution of village population hollowing; additionally, a regression equation model was established to identify factors influencing changes in the kinship spatial structure. The results have revealed: (1) The overall closeness of kinship ties in Yubu Village has decreased annually, with local stability declined, leading to a gradual loosening of traditional family connections; (2) The village’s overall spatial pattern has changed over time, showing sparse local distribution and varying degrees of change across six subgroups; (3) Kinship structure changes have been influenced by various factors including infrastructure, socioeconomic conditions, and cultural heritage, with dynamic evolution over time. From socioeconomic, infrastructure, and cultural heritage perspectives, future strategies have been proposed to guide ethnic village protection and contribute to the international literature of rural studies, providing valuable references for rural revitalization in ethnic regions of western China.

title: Dwelling without home: the aesthetics of belonging in post-disaster container settlements
abstract: In the aftermath of large-scale disasters, container settlements emerge as temporary shelters designed primarily for functionality and logistics. Yet, beyond their utilitarian intent, these environments evolve into symbolic terrains where individuals reconstruct meaning, identity, and belonging. This paper conceptualizes post-disaster container settlements as sociocultural texts that reveal how spatial order reflects both collective habitus and individual aesthetic agency. Drawing on Gaston Bachelard’s poetics of dwelling, Henri Lefebvre’s production of space, and Pierre Bourdieu’s theories of habitus and symbolic capital, the study reinterprets the notion of “temporary dwelling” as a process of social reproduction and adaptation rather than displacement. Methodologically, the research adopts a qualitative discourse and visual analysis, using publicly available documentation, media images, and institutional archives of container settlements in Türkiye. By bridging sociological and architectural thinking, this paper argues that belonging is not merely a product of physical permanence but an aesthetic and symbolic negotiation between structure and agency. The findings aim to reposition post-disaster architecture within the sociological understanding of place-making, emphasizing that even in transience, space functions as a site of identity formation and social continuity.

title: The semantic taxonomy of vulnerability: a bibliometric study using natural language processing
abstract: Abstract Vulnerability has become a central but conceptually diffuse term across the human and social sciences, used to designate heterogeneous risks, conditions, and causal processes. This conceptual dispersion hinders cumulative theorizing and limits the research’s capacity to inform policy and intervention. This article presents a reproducible, multi-resolution mapping of how vulnerability is organized in the scholarly literature, based on a Natural Language Processing pipeline that combines contextual keyword extraction, static keyword aggregation, data-driven dimensionality reduction, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering with Ward linkage. A Scopus search conducted in May 2025 identified 12,450 English-language journal articles in social science, psychology, arts and humanities, economics, and business with “vulnerability” in the title. The resulting dendrogram is reported across the full range k = [2, 12], and a further analysis inspects the specific k = 7 cut, at which seven semantic clusters emerge: psychopathology, health, rights and violence, climate and rural livelihood, floods and natural disasters, security and infrastructure, economic poverty, and pandemic and migration. Cluster quality is assessed through a multi-metric validation envelope that combines geometric fit with topic coherence. Three VosViewer keyword co-occurrence maps trace how the lexical landscape evolves across historically meaningful periods. Since 2000, climate- and disaster-related vulnerability has expanded sharply, while psychopathology-oriented research has lost relative prominence. The contribution is positioned as a methodologically transparent instrument for critical inquiry into how a contested concept is organized and how that organization changes over time.

title: Reflective interdisciplinarity in practice: integrating biology and philosophy in studies of individualization
abstract: Abstract Interdisciplinary research is widely acknowledged as a valuable means of knowledge production and as crucial for addressing complex scientific and societal problems. Interdisciplinary research takes many forms, and this article offers a novel case study of a distinctive form of interdisciplinarity, reflective interdisciplinarity. The article analyzes interdisciplinary research undertaken by philosophers of biology and empirically working biologists studying individualization. This kind of interdisciplinarity is reflective because biology is the target domain that philosophers of biology (and philosophically-minded biologists) reflect upon—as opposed to interdisciplinarity that occurs, for example, when insights from multiple distinct research domains are integrated. To analyze the case study, an analytic framework is developed that distinguishes four dimensions of interdisciplinarity: objects of interdisciplinary research, interdisciplinary research activities, communication of interdisciplinary results, and personal, institutional, and other conditions of interdisciplinary research. The case study shows, first, that reflective interdisciplinarity can involve interdependent, deeply immersive and cooperative interdisciplinary research processes (‘inquiry-embedded integration’) that include a form of knowledge-producing inquiry through which novel epistemic products emerge from joint commitments and goals, shared research questions, and intensive, collaborative discursive practices. The article adapts the notion of a plural subject in characterizing inquiry-embedded integration. Second, the analysis of the case study demonstrates how communicative choices, together with institutional and normative conditions, are partially constitutive of the interdisciplinary process. They shape the content of interdisciplinary products and play decisive roles in interdisciplinary activities such as knowledge integration. Finally, because the case study comprises the authors’ own research processes and publications, the analysis demonstrates that self-reflexive, qualitative analysis of interdisciplinary practice provides a valuable means of theorizing about interdisciplinarity with potential to offer transferable insights.

title: Governance or collusion? The dual effects of common institutional ownership on corporate greenwashing
abstract: Common institutional ownership occurs when the same institutional investor holds significant stakes in multiple competing companies within the same industry or market. This shared ownership can influence corporate behavior by either aligning or conflicting with managerial incentives, potentially fostering collaborative governance or collusive practices. Drawing on principal-agent theory, institutional theory, and the organizational economics view of governance structure adaptiveness, this study examines how different types of common institutional ownership affect corporate greenwashing. Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2011 to 2024, we find that long-term common institutional ownership significantly suppresses greenwashing, whereas short-term common institutional ownership significantly exacerbates it. Financing constraints and managerial myopia are two of the key mediating mechanisms. Long-term shared ownership appears to alleviate financing constraints and reduce managerial short-sightedness, which in turn suppresses greenwashing. Conversely, short-term shared ownership intensifies these issues, promoting greenwashing. Further heterogeneity analyses indicate that the constraining effect of long-term common institutional ownership is more pronounced in non-state-owned enterprises (non-SOEs) and firms with weak internal controls, whereas the promoting effect of short-term common institutional ownership is mainly concentrated in firms with weak internal controls. In addition, net-effect tests show that when both types of common owners coexist within the same firm, the governance effect of long-term common institutional ownership exerts a stronger overall influence on greenwashing. By distinguishing between long-term and short-term common institutional investors, this study provides more nuanced evidence on the governance consequences of common ownership and offers practical implications for improving green governance and promoting sustainable development.

title: Digital economy development, corporate key core technological innovation and new-quality productivity
abstract: This study examines the impacts of digital economy on corporate key core technological innovation and new-quality productivity, and explores the mechanism linking them. The results show that digital economy drives key core technological innovation and new-quality productivity. Key core technological innovation exerts a mediating effect while digital economy enhances new-quality productivity. Heterogeneity discussion indicates that in the eastern and central regions, and non-state-owned enterprises, digital economy promotes new-quality productivity and key core technological innovation. Compared to non-high-tech enterprises, digital economy has a more significant promoting effect on new-quality productivity in high-tech enterprises. The mechanism that digital economy promotes key core technological innovation and thereby enhances new-quality productivity is manifested in the eastern and central regions, non-state-owned enterprises, but not significantly in the western regions or state-owned enterprises. Finally, it is recommended that enterprises achieve key core technological breakthroughs, thereby cultivating new-quality productivity. According to corporate geographical locations, technological attributes, and property attributes, regulatory authorities provide differentiated policy support, to promote the effects of digital economy in empowering key core technological innovation and new-quality productivity. This study offers micro-evidence to assess the effectiveness of big data comprehensive pilot zone initiatives.

title: The cycle of atmosphere in The Garden of Evening Mists: a prison of trauma and a path to redemption
abstract: This study examines the dual role of atmosphere as both a carrier of trauma and a medium for healing in Tan Twan Eng’s The Garden of Evening Mists . Through a close textual analysis of the novel’s protagonist, Teoh Yun Ling, and the symbolic garden she inhabits, works in, and later alters, the paper explores how atmospheric elements—such as natural landscapes, sensory triggers, and spatial dynamics—simultaneously evoke traumatic memories and facilitate psychological reconciliation. Yun Ling’s journey suggests that trauma, though inescapable, may be partially reconfigured through deliberate engagement with the environment. The garden, initially a site of repressed memories and colonial violence, becomes a space where fragmented identity and historical pain are confronted and, at moments, provisionally reshaped. By analysing interactions between Yun Ling’s physical labour (gardening), sensory experiences (scents, sounds, and textures), and the garden’s decay and adaptation, the study demonstrates how atmosphere operates as a dynamic interface between memory and agency. The novel’s refusal to offer complete resolution underscores the notion that healing lies not in erasing trauma but in redefining its role within lived experience. The garden gestures toward what might be called a postcolonial coexistence, yet this remains partial, provisional, and always vulnerable to disruption.

title: Research on the spatio-temporal evolution of hidden thematic features in online public opinion: a case study of ethnic and religious perceptions in the Ding Zhen phenomenon
abstract: With the rapid development of social media, ethnic and religious public opinion—originating from geographically rooted issues—has increasingly spread and evolved online, resulting in more complex patterns of spatiotemporal evolution. Current research mainly focuses on dissemination and evolution mechanisms of public opinion information, with limited regard for the interactive evolutionary relationship and thematic features between offline geographical space and online network space. This study presents a framework for spatiotemporal evolution analysis and a latent topic analysis algorithm for public opinion on ethnic and religious affairs networks, considering both text space and geographical space, taking the example of ~25,000 pieces of all-media public opinion data on the “Ding Zhen popularity” event, using techniques such as spatial analysis, topic mining, and similarity comparison, explore the spatiotemporal distribution characteristics of online public opinion attention, analyze the content and intensity. The primary research findings indicate: 1. In terms of spatiotemporal evolution, network attention shows a prominent negative correlation pattern in space, hotspots are mainly concentrated in the central (e.g., Chengdu) and eastern (e.g., Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou) regions, with network connection presents a “point axis” pattern; 2. Concerning topic distribution, the latent topic analysis algorithm proposed in conjunction with geographical locations effectively discovers the distribution of public opinion topics, topic intensity, and content evolution patterns. The average accuracy improved by 13% compared to the LDA algorithm; 3. Examining the latent topic features mapped from text space to geographical space, the similarity of public opinion topics is unevenly distributed at the urban scale, indicating that factors such as regional race, religion, and economic status have a significant impact on the distribution of ethnic and religious public opinion.

title: Impact of the spatial correlation network of new quality productive forces on the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction
abstract: Against the backdrop of the “dual-carbon” strategy and comprehensive rural revitalization, exploring the impacts and underlying mechanisms of the spatial correlation network of new quality productive forces on the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction provides crucial references for green and low-carbon rural development. Based on a research sample of 30 Chinese provinces from 2010 to 2023, this paper systematically analyzes the transmission pathways through which the spatial correlation network of new quality productive forces affects the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction by employing a Double Machine Learning model. The empirical findings reveal that the level of the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction exhibited an upward trend over the study period, accompanied by pronounced spatial disparities. Furthermore, the spatial correlation network of new quality productive forces significantly promotes the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction, with prominent spatial spillover effects being detected. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the impacts of spatial correlation networks of new quality productive forces on the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction vary across four dimensions: temporal spans, resource endowments, human capital levels, and low-carbon lifestyles. Mechanism testing demonstrates that agricultural technological innovation plays a significant mediating role in the impact of the spatial correlation networks of new quality productive forces on the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction, with agricultural invention innovation serving as the primary pathway. Collectively, this study uncovers the intricate pathways of the synergistic effect of agricultural pollution and carbon reduction from the spatial correlation networks of new quality productive forces perspective, offering robust empirical evidence for the coordinated advancement of rural green development and the low-carbon economy.

title: Unlocking digital citizenship: a moderated mediator study on the power of social media literacy and age in teacher practices
abstract: Abstract The present study examines the complex relationships among teachers’ digital literacy, social media literacy, and digital citizenship, while accounting for age-based differences. A study was conducted utilizing data from 822 Turkish teachers. A moderated mediation model was employed to investigate the mediating role of social media literacy and the moderating role of age. The findings of the study indicated that digital literacy exhibited a positive correlation with digital citizenship, with social media literacy functioning as a significant mediator. Furthermore, the findings of this study demonstrate that age moderates the direct effect of digital literacy on digital citizenship, such that the effect is stronger among older teachers. However, it was observed that younger teachers exhibited higher levels of digital citizenship skills. The findings of this study indicate that enhancing digital literacy may help explain differences in civic engagement among different age groups. The study emphasises the significance of integrating targeted professional development programmes that cultivate both social media competence and equitable access to digital citizenship skills across generational cohorts. The implications of these findings are discussed in relation to inclusive educational policy and teacher development in digitally mediated learning environments.

title: The covariation between fear of missing out and mental health: based on a parallel-process latent growth curve model
abstract: Fear of missing out (FoMO) has become a common emotion that has a strong relation with mental health, while their covariation remains unclear. The study aimed to investigate the covariation between FoMO and mental health and to identify the dimension of mental health (including depression, anxiety and stress) most relevant to FoMO. A total of 542 college students ( M age = 19.72 ± 2.28 years old) participated in the three-wave assessment study, spaced over a two-week period. They were required to complete the Fear of Missing Out Scale (FoMOs), the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and the background questionnaire. Parallel-process latent growth curve models were used to explore the covariation between FoMO and mental health (including depression, anxiety and stress). The results showed that the FoMO intercept was positively correlated with the intercepts of mental health and its three dimensions. The slope of FoMO was positively associated with the slopes of mental health and the stress dimension. The intercept of FoMO negatively predicted the slopes of mental health and the stress dimension. In conclusion, the study highlights that FoMO covaries with mental health, especially with the stress dimension. Further interventions could focus on reducing FoMO and stress. This might decrease the risk of depression and anxiety, thereby improving mental health.

title: A practicable comprehensive assessment system for evaluating Debt2Health swap recipients: guiding donor decision-making
abstract: Debt2Health (D2H) swap is an innovative financing tool that addresses public health funding gaps in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) facing debt distress. China, Qatar, South Korea, the United Kingdom, and Portugal are major creditors to LMICs and active global health actors, yet none have participated in D2H swaps. The study (using data from 2021) proposes a multi-dimensional assessment framework, health performance was rated as the most critical factor, followed by bilateral relations, environmental performance, political feasibility, and debt vulnerability. Using the entropy-weighted TOPSIS (Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution) method, the countries that had previously implemented D2H (Pakistan, Egypt, Cameroon and Jordan) emerged as the top recipient candidates. Comoros and Algeria stood out among the new potential candidates. According to some senior experts via AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process), Pakistan and Egypt are China’s most desirable recipients. Furthermore, in the future, other potential D2H donor countries may invite their own experts to participate in our designed questionnaire surveys or evaluation systems to screen viable recipient nations and enhance the success of D2H. This approach establishes a robust basis for fostering diverse, equitable and mutually beneficial international cooperation, incorporating both South-South and North-South partnerships to promote global health and development.

title: A proposed model for predicting the intention to use the metaverse in computer programming education
abstract: Abstract The advent of new technologies has significantly increased digitalization in education by accelerating the shift to digital products and tools. In particular, notable innovations in artificial intelligence and Metaverse technologies hold promising potential to transform educational and training formats globally, demanding swift reforms in education systems. This study explored the factors influencing the adoption of Metaverse-based software among 640 students pursuing associate degrees in computer programming within the framework of the extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). While previous research has explored general factors influencing technology adoption, gaps remain regarding the specific role of perceived complexity, enjoyment, and student self-efficacy within technical education contexts. The model designed to explain students’ behavioral intentions toward Metaverse-based technologies was analyzed and validated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The study findings indicated that students’ perceived ease of use (PEOU) and perceived usefulness (PU) significantly influenced their behavioral intentions (BI) regarding the Metaverse. Among the external factors included in the model, it was determined that social influence (SIE), peer influence (PIE), and personal innovativeness (PI) variables significantly affected PU. In contrast, the perceived complexity (PC) variable significantly impacted PEOU and PU. This article examines the opportunities and challenges that Metaverse technologies bring to learning in computer programming studies and discusses the proposed research model for explaining students’ behavioral intentions. The study aims to develop new approaches that can offer significant opportunities in this field by establishing a framework for future research on the applications of the Metaverse in education.

title: Digital welfare or hidden price: short videos, happiness, and the digital Inclusion
abstract: There is an ongoing debate about whether digital technologies deliver welfare gains or introduce hidden costs. Evidence on the welfare effects of rapidly growing short-video platforms, especially for digitally disadvantaged groups in China is limited. This study examines the association between short-video use and subjective happiness using the China Family Panel Studies 2020–2022 panel ( N = 22,282). Employing two-way fixed-effects models and multiple robustness tests, we find that moderate short-video use is associated with higher self-reported happiness. Heterogeneity analysis shows stronger impact for digitally disadvantaged groups, including rural residents especially seniors, older adults especially without companion and less-educated. Mechanism tests point to emotional companionship and social trust, driven by enhanced information access. These findings suggest that short videos may serve as a low-cost means to promote happiness and digital inclusion.

title: Do environmental regulations moderate the impact of FDI on emissions in Sub-Saharan Africa?
abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) confronts a pressing trade-off between attracting foreign direct investment (FDI) to stimulate economic development and curbing the associated rise in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. However, empirical evidence on whether environmental regulation can effectively mitigate the environmental footprint of FDI remains limited and inconclusive, particularly across SSA’s diverse institutional and income settings. This study examines whether environmental regulation moderates the FDI-emissions nexus and how this relationship varies across subregions, income levels, and time horizons. We analyse a balanced panel of 42 SSA countries from 2005 to 2023, employing Panel-Corrected Standard Errors (PCSE) as the primary estimator, with Driscoll–Kraay, instrumental variables, and Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG) methods for robustness. FDI exerts a positive and significant effect on GHG emissions ( β = 0.411, p < 0.001), confirming the pollution haven hypothesis (H1). Stronger environmental regulation directly reduces emissions ( β = −0.522, p < 0.001) (H2) and, crucially, negatively moderates the FDI-emissions relationship ( β = −3.920, p < 0.001) (H3). The Environmental Kuznets Curve is validated, with a turning point of USD 3545 PPP (H4). Subregionally, the moderating effect is strongest in West and East Africa; by income group, it is most effective in low- and upper-middle-income countries. Theoretically, the study integrates pollution haven and ecological modernisation frameworks by demonstrating that environmental regulatory stringency (ERS) conditions the environmental outcomes of FDI. Policy implications underscore the need for strengthened regulatory enforcement, income-differentiated interventions, and enhanced regional cooperation to decouple FDI-driven growth from environmental degradation.

title: Flood-induced displacement and resilience: the mediating role of coping strategies within the sustainable livelihood framework
abstract: Abstract Flood-induced displacement has become a critical challenge in disaster-prone areas particularly in low-income countries where communities depend entirely on the natural resources. This study examines how various forms of livelihood capital such as natural, physical, human, social and financial capital affect livelihood resilience among flood-displaced households, and the mediating role of coping behaviors. Using the Sustainable Livelihood Framework and resilience theory, the study employs partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine the survey data from 590 displaced farming households. Findings show that flood-induced displacement significantly depletes livelihood capitals, thereby constraining households’ adaptive capacity. Social and natural capitals exhibit the strongest relative contributions to livelihood resilience, followed by financial and human capital, whereas physical capital shows a comparatively weaker effect. Coping behavior serves as a key mediating mechanism that transforms available capital into resilience outcomes. The study further proposes capital ranking strategies as an innovative analytical tool to compare the relative influence of different livelihood capitals rather than as a prescriptive prioritization approach. By reconceptualizing coping behavior as a mediator variable, rather than an outcome variable, this study contributes to the livelihood resilience theory. It offers empirically grounded insights for policymakers, development practitioners, and humanitarian agencies designing targeted resettlement, sustainable intervention, and recovery initiatives.

title: Transdisciplinary doctoral schools—What capabilities do we need to master collaborative science-society interactions in transformative research?
abstract: In the face of severe socio-ecological crises, there is a growing consensus that research has a responsibility to engage actors within and beyond academia to create actionable knowledge for supporting the transformation towards sustainability. As a result, transdisciplinarity, characterized by the collaboration of actors that transgress disciplines and sectors, has become an important approach. However, applying transdisciplinary research approaches implies the mastery of often complex science-society interactions that require a variety of capabilities. Emerging transdisciplinary doctoral schools could be places where the next generation of transdisciplinary researchers is equipped with this necessary expertise. However, designing appropriate curricula is challenging because of heterogeneous understandings of what is needed to master transdisciplinary processes between science and policy, but also between different scientific communities. To date, there is no consolidated knowledge about what capabilities are considered important for pursuing transdisciplinary careers. To close this knowledge gap, a Q-study was conducted with 59 PhD candidates, alumni, and faculty members from three consecutive installments of a transdisciplinary-oriented doctoral school. Participants ranked the importance of 36 statements about capabilities identified as relevant for transdisciplinary approaches in the literature. Analysis revealed four distinct viewpoints, each emphasizing different capabilities: (i) being open to integrating different perspectives; (ii) being methodologically grounded; (iii) producing actionable knowledge; (iv) creating respectful and empathic interactions. In addition, findings indicate that PhD candidates and faculty members diverge in their views, and that capabilities focused on long-term career development and community building are universally considered less important. To deal with the heterogeneity of views, transdisciplinary doctoral schools should engage in expectation management and offer a flexible curriculum that conveys core messages of transdisciplinarity to all candidates while still providing opportunities for specialization. Moreover, doctoral schools should be seen not only as places for acquiring personal competencies, but also as places for building careers and communities.

title: Spatial distribution patterns and influencing factors of rural settlements in Lhasa, Tibet
abstract: Abstract As a central hub on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, Lhasa exhibits unique rural settlement patterns shaped by harsh high-altitude environments, economic disparities, and profound socio-cultural influences. To elucidate the underlying formation mechanisms, this study constructs a “Nature-Economy-Culture” tripartite framework. Using data from 226 villages, we established an integrated workflow encompassing pattern identification, driver detection, and mechanism modeling. Methodologies included spatial statistics, Geodetector, Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), and XGBoost-SHAP analysis to investigate the influencing factors of settlement distribution. Results show:: (1) The spatial distribution presents a significant differentiation pattern characterized by “two high-density clusters, one axial belt, and multiple scattered points”; (2) Settlement density exhibits significant spatial coupling with natural, economic, and cultural factors; (3) Elevation ( q = 0.553), cultural heritage density ( q = 0.439) and precipitation ( q = 0.216) were identified as the primary determinants driving spatial heterogeneity, demonstrating distinct threshold and mutual enhancement effects; and (4) These factors exert spatially heterogeneous influences, shaping local patterns by modulating the explanatory power of variables across different sub-regions. This study contributes to research on human-land relationships in high-altitude regions and provides a scientific basis for rural spatial optimization and cultural landscape conservation.

title: Linguistic manipulation and behavioural patterns of stalking: a case analysis in Malaysia
authors: Nur Baneen Natasya Mohd Fairul Aswan
abstract: Stalking has become an increasingly recognised concern in Malaysia since its criminalisation in 2023, yet its early manifestations often remain difficult to identify because they are embedded in ordinary, informal digital interaction. Defined as repeated and unauthorised intrusion into an individual’s life, stalking frequently unfolds through conversational practices that appear benign, socially acceptable, and relationally oriented. While existing research has examined stalking from behavioural, psychological, and legal perspectives, limited attention has been given to the linguistic mechanisms through which manipulation is enacted in everyday interaction. This study addresses this gap through a forensic-pragmatic analysis of authentic online conversations between a stalker and a victim. Drawing on a dataset of 33,929 words collected over a 60-day period, the analysis examines how routine conversational practices function interactionally to sustain access, normalise persistence, and erode relational boundaries over time. The findings identify a set of overlapping interactional patterns, including superficial normalcy, repeated offers and invitations, trust-building practices, excessive concern, and the emergence of surveillance-indexing knowledge claims. These patterns do not operate as fixed stages or overtly coercive acts, but co-occur and intensify cumulatively within an apparently benign conversational frame. The study further demonstrates how localised features of Malaysian English, such as discourse particles and localised tense marking, function as interactional resources that project familiarity and shared identity, contributing to the construction of pseudo-intimacy. To account for these dynamics, the study proposes the Malaysian English-based Linguistic Stalking and Localised Speech (MELLS) framework as an analytical scaffold for examining linguistic manipulation in digitally mediated stalking contexts, advancing linguistic approaches to technology-facilitated harm and offering tools relevant to forensic analysis and early intervention.

title: Examining the evolving geography of innovation and its divergent patterns within Chinese cities
abstract: This study typologizes the evolving geography of innovation within Chinese cities. The analysis characterizes innovation activities based on patent applications, employs a large-scale dataset of more than nine million patent records, and covers 234 Chinese cities for 2009–2020. The distribution of patent applications within cities is measured based on polycentricity, dispersion, and size of innovation centers. Employing hierarchical clustering and a decision tree model, the analysis clusters cities based on evolving spatial structures of innovation and associates these clusters with relevant socioeconomic factors. While the distribution of innovation activities has become more polycentric and less dispersed within Chinese cities, the study identifies six modes of spatial structural changes. Each mode reflects a distinctive evolution pattern of polycentricity, dispersion, and center size.

title: ICT and governance as moderators: enhancing the social returns of logistics performance for sustainable human development in the GCC
abstract: This study examines the conditional relationship between logistics performance and sustainable human development in the resource‑rich Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). Moving beyond direct effects, it proposes and tests a contingency framework in which Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and, more critically, Institutional Quality (IQ) serve as key moderators that enhance the social returns of logistics infrastructure. Using robust panel data techniques on a 2007–2022 GCC dataset, the analysis confirms logistics performance as a significant driver of the Human Development Index. The primary finding is the positive moderating role of Institutional Quality, which is larger in magnitude than that of ICT. This underscores the necessity of robust governance, rule of law, and effective regulation in transforming logistical efficiency into equitable advancements in health, education, and income. The research contributes theoretically by advancing a model of synergistic socio‑technical‑institutional systems for development and provides a clear policy imperative. For GCC planners and similar economies, achieving sustainable development requires an integrated approach that aligns logistics modernization with digital transformation and comprehensive institutional reform, as investments in infrastructure alone fall short of delivering optimal human development outcomes.

title: From interpersonal competence to willingness to communicate in Turkish: the mediating roles of speaking self-efficacy and intercultural engagement
abstract: This study investigates how interpersonal communication competence (ICC) relates to second language (L2) willingness to communicate (WTC) through the parallel mediating roles of L2 speaking self-efficacy (SSE) and intercultural interaction engagement (IIE) among learners of Turkish as a foreign language. Using data from 486 international students enrolled in Turkish language programs at universities in Türkiye, the hypothesized model was tested via structural equation modeling. The results revealed that ICC was positively associated with WTC both directly and indirectly. Specifically, SSE and IIE each carried a significant indirect association between ICC and WTC, supporting a partial-mediation pattern. Among the proximal predictors, SSE showed the strongest direct association with WTC, followed by IIE, while ICC retained a smaller but significant direct association. The model explained 73.7% of the variance in WTC. These findings highlight the importance of target-language-specific efficacy beliefs and intercultural motivation in linking general communication competence to L2 communicative intent.

title: Designing a learning ecosystem for intangible cultural heritage in short-term study abroad: an outcome-based education case study
abstract: In the context of globalization, short-term study abroad (STSA) programs offer opportunities for Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) transmission, yet they often risk devolving into superficial cultural exposure. Addressing this design challenge, this study proposes a learning ecosystem model grounded in Outcome-Based Education (OBE) principles to support coherent and meaningful ICH learning within compressed timeframes. Using a design-oriented case study, the paper examines a 14-day Chinese ICH program for Thai vocational students to demonstrate how OBE can be operationalized at the program level. The proposed model consists of four interconnected components, each fulfilling a specific design function: the Ecosystem Core (institutional mission and vision, anchoring design priorities and value coherence); Ecosystem Architecture (reverse-designing educational objectives, learning outcomes, and curriculum to ensure structural alignment); Ecosystem Feedback (employing assessment and rubrics as self-regulating mechanisms to support adaptive adjustment); and Ecosystem Sustenance (maintaining coherence through responsive implementation and continuous evaluation). The case analysis shows how language learning, experiential engagement with ICH, investigative activities, and social interaction are systematically connected through this ecosystem design. The study contributes theoretically by extending OBE from course-level outcome alignment to ecosystem-level design logic, and practically by offering a transferable framework to guide vocational institutions in developing context-sensitive STSA programs that promote sustainable ICH education and international cooperation.

title: From undifferentiated to defined: a mixed-methods, data-driven investigation of the acculturation of culturally undifferentiated majority members
abstract: Abstract In increasingly diverse societies, people in intercultural contact must navigate cultural diversity to find their place and sense of belonging. Yet, research on acculturation has largely focused on minority groups, leaving majority group responses to cultural change underexplored. A substantial subset of majority group members adopts an undifferentiated acculturation strategy, expressing low or neutral scores on both heritage culture maintenance and other culture adoption. This pre-registered mixed-methods study provides the first comprehensive examination of this strategy’s internal heterogeneity. We surveyed 316 undifferentiated White British participants and applied Latent Profile Analysis across psychological, ideological, and demographic variables, integrating these results with quantified qualitative data. The analysis revealed two subgroups. The larger Humanistic profile ( n = 242) was characterised by politically liberal views, stronger identification with all humanity, and inclusive attitudes towards immigrants, and scored significantly higher—though still neutral in absolute terms—on other culture adoption. Their neutrality appeared to reflect a universalist, equality-oriented outlook rather than indifference, suggesting a cosmopolitan form of belonging grounded in global human identification. The smaller Detached profile ( n = 74) showed higher cultural-identity reflection and cultural essentialism, and greater indifference to intercultural contact, but did not differ from the Humanistic group on heritage culture maintenance. This orientation reflected a more disengaged or ambivalent sense of belonging, marked by scepticism towards cultural identity as a basis for social connection. These findings demonstrate that the undifferentiated strategy is not monolithic but comprises at least two orientations: one grounded in inclusive, humanity-based belonging and another reflecting detachment from cultural involvement. We propose extending acculturation theory to incorporate these humanistic and detached patterns, which may represent distinct adaptations to culturally complex, globalised societies. We discuss their implications for fostering or hindering belonging among a substantial segment of majority-group members.

title: Analysis of innovative strategies to alleviate the influence of COVID-19 on sustainable supply chain performance: PLS-SEM and deep learning artificial neural network analysis
abstract: Abstract The worldwide spread of the COVID-19 epidemic caused significant upheavals, especially impacting supply chain (SC) systems. Addressing these issues requires the development of creative and novel approaches. Therefore, this study investigates how digital innovation (DI), information processing capability (IPC), and supply chain integration (SCI) alleviate the influence of the COVID-19 epidemic on sustainable supply chain performance (SSCP). The study also examines the mediating roles of DI, IPC, and SCI and the moderating role of institutional support (IS). Data were gathered from Pakistani food supply chain enterprises and employed a two-phase method integrating partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and artificial neural network (ANN) techniques. The result reveals that while COVID-19 disruption negatively impacted SSCP, it positively influenced DI, IPC, and SCI. Moreover, DI, IPC, and SCI intervene in the link between COVID-19 disruption and SSCP. Institutional support strengthens the favorable effects of DI, IPC, and SCI on SSCP. Drawing on the resource-based view, dynamic capability theory, and organizational information processing theory, this study explains how firms can improve resilience and sustainability during disruptions. This model offers potential strategies for managers and policymakers to enhance supply chain resilience and maintain performance in the face of crises.

title: Flood risk under sea-level rise and lessons on adaptation policies in coastal urban management: a case study in Hai Phong City, Vietnam
abstract: Abstract Climate change and sea-level rise are increasing flood risks in coastal urban areas, including those in Vietnam. Hai Phong city, one of the most important coastal urban areas in Vietnam, has been suffering significant impacts from frequent flooding caused by rising sea levels and rapid urbanization. This study examines the level of flood risk and identifies gaps in Hai Phong’s adaptive capacity by analyzing empirical data from two sea level monitoring stations (Hon Dau and Bach Long Vi, 2014–2023), vulnerability indices (VI), flood risk indices (FRI), and institutional SWOT analysis. The findings indicate a high level of vulnerability (VI = 3.61/5) and a considerable flood risk (FRI = 0.53), particularly in coastal areas, inner-city zones, and peri-urban transition regions. Simultaneously, the study also reveals substantial limitations in local adaptive capacity, particularly regarding institutions, planning, infrastructure, and resource mobilization mechanisms. Bearing this in mind, the study draws on successful adaptation models from Japan, Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand and highlights the effectiveness of integrated policies combining structural and non-structural measures, community participation, and intersectoral coordination. These lessons may support Hai Phong in developing a flexible, spatially and temporally adaptive action road map that integrates risk management into urban planning and governance, thereby enhancing resilience and promoting sustainable development in the face of escalating climate change impacts.

title: The effects of flipped English course design on students’ achievement emotion, self-efficacy belief, learning responsibility, and interactions with their teachers
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of English teaching based on the flipped learning (FL) model on students’ English self-efficacy beliefs, achievement emotions, learning responsibilities, teacher-student interaction, and academic achievement. The research employed a mixed-method intervention design with 30 ninth-grade students from an Anatolian high school in Sivas, Türkiye, and the study group was randomly assigned. Before the intervention, a pretest was administered regarding academic achievement, English self-efficacy belief, learning responsibility, teacher-student interaction, and achievement emotions. The researcher kept a research diary during the application process. After the intervention, a posttest was conducted, and semi-structured interviews were held to obtain the students’ opinions about the application. The findings indicated that significant increases were observed in students’ English academic achievement and several positive achievement emotions following the intervention, while significant decreases were observed in negative emotions ( p < 0.05). However, it did not produce a significant effect on course-related hope and pride ( p > 0.05). In addition, it was observed that the FL model effectively increased students’ English self-efficacy beliefs, learning responsibilities, and interactions with their teachers ( p < 0.05). Qualitative data supported these findings. According to the students’ opinions, it was found that FL motivated students to take an active part in class, particularly in speaking activities, and engaged them in lessons. It enabled students to have firm self-efficacy beliefs and take responsibility for their learning. While FL increased positive emotions, it decreased the negative emotions of students toward the lesson. Besides, it positively affected the interactions between students and the teacher. Overall, the findings suggest that the FL model may contribute to improvements in several cognitive and emotional learning outcomes in this specific context.

title: The economic impact of COVID-19: losses and resilience factors
abstract: This study proposes a numerical assessment of the economic loss associated with COVID-19 across 46 countries. We estimate these losses by forecasting each country’s counterfactual GDP, that is, the GDP that would have occurred in the absence of the pandemic, using a hybrid WT–QPSO–ANFIS model. Comparing the forecasted values with actual GDP in 2020–2021 allows us to quantify the economic consequences associated with the pandemic. The results show that the hybrid model delivers the best predictive performance relative to conventional forecasting approaches and indicates average GDP growth reductions of 6.32% in 2020 and 2.87% in 2021. To further examine cross-country differences in these outcomes, we analyze macroeconomic and pandemic-related factors associated with economic loss using panel regression analysis. The findings suggest that higher government debt, lower foreign exchange reserves, and stricter containment measures are associated with larger economic losses, while higher vaccination rates are associated with lower losses.

title: Correction: The endangered Tanka language in Hong Kong: phonological variations and lexical convergence with Cantonese
abstract: Correction to: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-025-05417-3 , published online 19 July 2025

title: Conceptualizing fear in Saudi Arabic and English: a cross-cultural metaphorical analysis
abstract: The study investigates how fear is metaphorically conceptualized in Saudi Arabic and English, identifying both shared and culture-specific patterns based on Conceptual Metaphor Theory (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980) and Kövecses’ metaphorical framing (2000). The study adopts a qualitative, lexical–conceptual approach to analyze naturally occurring discourse. A purpose-built bilingual dataset of 100 metaphorical expressions (46 Saudi Arabic and 54 English) was compiled and analyzed in context to ensure cross-linguistic comparability. The findings reveal substantial convergence in core embodied metaphors of fear across the two languages, including mappings structured around force, bodily disruption, containment, and loss of control. At the same time, systematic differences emerge in how these shared mappings are elaborated. Saudi Arabic expressions tend to highlight somatic impact, anatomical specificity, and visibly embodied reactions, whereas English expressions more often emphasize internalized, perceptual, or cognitive responses. These contrasts reflect differences in how shared metaphors are elaborated and expressed in language. By distinguishing shared conceptual metaphors from language-specific patterns of elaboration, the study contributes to contrastive metaphor research on colloquial Saudi Arabic and supports a more discourse-sensitive application of Conceptual Metaphor Theory. The findings also have practical implications for Arabic–English translation and language education, particularly in contexts where similar emotional meanings are conveyed through non-corresponding metaphorical cues.

title: Is taxi a net substitute or complement for public transit? Evidence from high-granularity taxi GPS data
abstract: This research investigates the spatial and temporal relationship between taxi and public transit usage in order to probe the role of taxi in facilitating public transit and enhancing transport sustainability. By geographically aggregating large volumes of high-granularity taxi GPS data from New York City into block-group level metrics and integrating with a variety of built environment features and socio-economic factors, we apply spatial econometrics models. We find that public transit coverage (subway and bus) in a neighborhood has positive impacts on the number of taxi drop-offs during morning peak hours and taxi pick-ups during evening peak hours, both in that neighborhood locally and in its surrounding neighborhoods. These positive direct and spillover effects are statistically significant after controlling for employment density. This research has important policy implications on how the growing on-demand ride-sourcing services should be regulated to reinforce their complementary role to public transit, enhance transit ridership, and promote transport sustainability.

title: Correction: Investigating the impact of decent work perception on employee voice behavior: evidence from text mining

title: Digital and intelligent policy instrument portfolio and green transformation of cities: evidence from China
abstract: In the digital-economy era, can policies represented by the national big data comprehensive pilot zones and the smart city pilot program work in tandem to effectively foster urban green development? Using panel data for 251 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2006-2022 and a staggered DID model, this paper evaluates the multidimensional impacts of “digital-intelligent” policy collaboration on regional green transition. The findings are as follows: first, the dual-pilot policy significantly raises green total factor productivity in pilot cities, promotes local green transition, and generates marked green spatial spillovers; Second, the green co-empowerment effect of digital-intelligent policies is closely tied to regional characteristics and is further shaped by talent agglomeration and the strength of intellectual property protection; Third, mechanism analysis shows that the collaboration advances urban green development by improving energy consumption levels, enhancing digital technological innovation capacity, and strengthening industrial agglomeration; Fourth, heterogeneity analysis indicates that the empowering effect is more pronounced in regions with higher digital-economy development, stronger new-energy transitions, greater fiscal capacity, and service-oriented industrial structures; Fifth, further evidence shows that the empowering effect is strongest when green technological innovation surpasses a certain level and environmental regulation is of moderate intensity. In addition, compared with single pilots, dual pilots better promote urban green transition, and a sequencing strategy that implements “digital” before “intelligent” achieves superior outcomes. These results offer important guidance for local governments to coordinate multi-policy portfolios, harness synergistic policy effects, and accelerate economy-wide green transition.

title: Cross-modal integration and asymmetry mechanisms in facial-vocal attractiveness evaluation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Facial and vocal attractiveness, as key dimensions of interpersonal perception, are evaluated through mechanisms that involve core cognitive processes of multisensory integration. Clarifying the strength and direction of their association can both reveal the cognitive basis of cross-modal impression formation and provide behavioral guidance for real-world scenarios such as social interaction and decision-making. However, existing research shows significant discrepancies regarding their correlation, and systematic evaluations verifying their relationship are lacking. This study aims to explore the correlation and asymmetry mechanisms between facial and vocal attractiveness in evaluations through a systematic review and meta-analysis, as well as to investigate potential moderating factors. Following the PRISMA guidelines and the standards proposed by Downs and Black (1998), 23 empirical studies were included in the meta-analysis, encompassing a total sample size of 4902. A random-effects model was used to calculate the pooled correlation coefficient (r) and 95% confidence interval (CI), followed by subgroup analyses to examine potential moderating variables impacting the observed differences. Finally, publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s linear regression, and sensitivity analyses were conducted. The results showed a significant positive correlation between facial and vocal attractiveness evaluations (r = 0.255, 95% CI [0.198, 0.311]), though subgroup analyses revealed this correlation was significant only for female targets (r = 0.304, 95% CI [0.174, 0.425]) and not for male targets (r = 0.029, 95% CI [−0.114, 0.170]). Subgroup analyses further indicated that variables such as gender, age, hormone levels, cultural background, and stimulus characteristics moderated the correlation between the two forms of attractiveness. Despite detecting slight publication bias, the results remained robust and reliable after testing for bias and sensitivity. This study confirms the presence of cross-modal integration effects of facial and vocal attractiveness in interpersonal evaluation or impression formation, as well as asymmetry mechanisms characterized by gender differences. Qualitative synthesis of the broader literature further suggests a possible visual dominance effect, though direct quantitative evidence remains limited.

title: Ownership concentration and operational efficiency in emerging markets: the moderating role of market volatility
abstract: This study examines the relationship between ownership concentration, stock price volatility, and firm-level operational efficiency in an emerging market using a sample of 86 Saudi-listed firms from 2016 to 2023.
