Drawing on an interpretivist paradigm, qualitative data were collected from 21 in-depth interviews and 123 online travel posts, and analysed through content analysis and grounded theory to inductively derive the structure and mechanisms of intensity. The findings indicate five interrelated dimensions of sports event tourism intensity—time investment, physical exertion, travel interaction, cognitive engagement, and sensory stimulation—and further reveal two motivational drivers, fear of missing out and maximising travel value, that encourage tourists to voluntarily engage in high-intensity travel experiences. Rather than functioning as a direct determinant of tourist experience, sports event tourism intensity influences emotional outcomes through the development of tourism fatigue, comprising both physical and mental fatigue. Building on these findings and informed by Optimal Stimulation Level Theory, the study develops an interpretive mid-range framework illustrating how motivational drivers, sports event tourism intensity, tourism fatigue, and tourist experience interact throughout sports event tourism. The research contributes theoretically by complementing existing destination-level understandings of tourism intensity with an individual-level perspective, clarifying the distinction between sources of load and their experiential consequences, and extending current theorisation of sports event tourism experience. Practically, it offers insights for organisers and destination managers to design balanced itineraries, optimise infrastructure, and foster emotionally rewarding experiences by aligning stimulation with tourists’ recovery needs.

title: What role does healthcare geographic accessibility play in the association between personal health responsibility and family doctor contract services?
abstract: Abstract Background Limited research has examined the nexus between personal health responsibility and family doctor contract services, particularly the moderating role of healthcare geographic accessibility in this relationship. This study aimed to investigate the association between personal health responsibility and family doctor contract services and to determine how healthcare geographic accessibility shapes this relationship among rural older adults in China. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted from July to August 2022 in Shandong Province in China. A total of 3,164 rural older adults were included in the analysis. Multivariable binary logistic regression models and the margins plot were used for the moderating effect analysis. Results The rates of signing up for family doctor contract services and support for personal health responsibility among rural older adults in Shandong Province were 64.85% and 61.54%, respectively. Participants who supported personal health responsibility were more likely to contract for family doctor services (OR = 1.38, 95% CI = 1.13–1.69) after controlling for confounding factors. Only among older adults with good healthcare geographic accessibility, personal health responsibility was associated with higher contracting rates for family doctor services (OR = 1.48, 95% CI = 1.20–1.82). Conclusions Our findings reveal a correlation between personal health responsibility and engagement with family doctor contract services, with healthcare geographic accessibility serving as a pivotal moderating factor. It is imperative for governmental authorities to amplify targeted educational campaigns and outreach for rural older adults. Elevating their understanding of personal health responsibilities and enhancing healthcare geographic accessibility are crucial steps to encourage their participation in family doctor services.

title: Crisis to resilience: tracing direct, indirect and induced tourism impacts in Kenya’s economy
abstract: Tourism shocks can propagate well beyond visitor-facing industries through production networks, factor incomes, and household consumption. This study estimates the economy-wide effects of the COVID-19 tourism shock in Kenya using the Kenya Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) 2019 and publicly available Kenya Social Accounting Matrices (SAMs). Separate product-level final-demand shocks are constructed for inbound and domestic tourism in 2020 and 2021 relative to the 2019 benchmark. The combined visitor-demand contraction is estimated at KSh338.8 billion in 2020 and KSh174.2 billion in 2021. Using the 2019 Kenya SAM, these shocks generate estimated economy-wide gross-output contractions of KSh770.8 billion and KSh408.8 billion, respectively, alongside factor-value-added effects of KSh396.1 billion and KSh206.8 billion. Direct tourism employment-equivalent contractions are estimated at approximately 508,000 positions in 2020 and 249,000 in 2021. Inbound tourism accounts for most of the persistent 2021 shortfall, while domestic tourism recovers substantially faster. Transportation, accommodation, and food services experience the largest effects, with sizeable spillovers into trade, processed foods, agriculture, and business services. Structural sensitivity analysis using the 2021 Kenya SAM yields approximately 10% lower gross-output effects while preserving the direction and principal sectoral ranking of the findings. The results demonstrate both Kenya’s vulnerability to external tourism-demand shocks and the value of domestic tourism resilience, supporting policies that strengthen domestic and regional markets, supply-chain resilience, economic diversification, and inclusive crisis-response mechanisms.

title: AI-assisted speaking practice for EFL learners: effects on anxiety, enjoyment, and engagement compared to traditional teacher-led practice
abstract: Abstract Although recent studies have demonstrated the potential of AI chatbots in reducing foreign language speaking anxiety (FLSA) and enhancing positive emotions, significant gaps remain in the literature. Most previous research has examined anxiety, enjoyment, and engagement in isolation, with few studies investigating their dynamic interplay within a single intervention. Moreover, speaking, the skill most susceptible to anxiety, has received comparatively less attention in AI intervention research compared to writing. To address these gaps, this quasi-experimental study compares AI-assisted and teacher-led English speaking practice in their effects on Chinese EFL learners’ foreign language speaking anxiety (FLSA), foreign language enjoyment (FLE), and L2 engagement. Seventy-one first-year undergraduates from two intact classes were nonrandomly allocated to an EG ( n = 36; AI chatbot practice) or a control group ( n = 35; teacher-led practice) and followed the same 12-week syllabus. The EG practiced speaking with an AI chatbot, whereas the control group completed parallel activities under teacher guidance. Pretest–posttest surveys assessed FLSA, FLE, and engagement. One-way ANCOVAs that controlled for baseline scores showed a significant reduction in posttest speaking anxiety for the AI group relative to the control. Both groups reported gains in FLE and engagement; however, between-group differences on these two outcomes were not statistically significant. Within-group analyses indicated a significant decline in anxiety and substantial improvements in FLE and engagement for the AI group, while the control group showed only modest gains in engagement. Overall, the results suggest that AI chatbots can meaningfully reduce FLSA and bolster positive emotional engagement, consistent with Positive Psychology perspectives. Pedagogically, integrating AI tools into speaking curricula may help create a low-pressure, interactive environment that balances anxiety reduction with enjoyment-enhancing strategies, thereby fostering more resilient and engaged EFL learners.

title: Forecasting the volatility of WTI crude oil futures: a new perspective from uncertain threshold HAR models
abstract: The threshold heterogeneous autoregressive (THAR) model, by introducing a threshold mechanism, partitions volatility into different intervals, especially providing more refined treatment for extreme volatility parts, thereby compensating to some extent for the deficiencies of the traditional HAR model. However, in the complex and ever-changing financial market environment, the assumption of random residuals in the traditional THAR model often fails to hold, which significantly restricts the model’s applicability. Moreover, the model mainly relies on specific data characteristics to depict volatility while neglecting the intrinsic structure of the data, which, to some degree, weakens the model’s predictive accuracy and stability. To overcome the aforementioned issues, this paper constructs two uncertain THAR models based on uncertainty theory: one is the uncertain THAR model based on uncertain residuals (UR-UTHAR), and the other is the uncertain THAR model under imprecise data conditions (UV-UTHAR). Corresponding parameter estimations for these models are also provided. This paper takes the volatility of WTI crude oil futures as the research object for volatility prediction. By employing three randomness testing methods, this paper comprehensively verifies the limitations of the traditional THAR model in complex market environments. Meanwhile, using various out-of-sample evaluation methods, the significant advantages of the proposed models over traditional models in terms of predictive accuracy and stability are further demonstrated. Finally, by investigating the applicability of the models under three major event shocks: the global financial crisis, international crude oil price shocks, and the COVID-19 pandemic, the above conclusions are further consolidated, proving the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed models under different conditions.

title: Large language models as travel co-planners: the GIFT model of youth–AI interaction
abstract: This study examines how members of Generation Z and Generation Alpha perceive and use LLMs in tourism planning. Drawing on six age-specific focus groups with 57 participants (26 Generation Alpha pupils aged 11–14 and 31 Generation Z BSc students aged 20–24) conducted in Budapest, Hungary, the study uses a qualitative, Grounded Theory–informed approach to explore prior use, anticipated practices, credibility assessments, and the meanings attached to LLMs. Participants in both cohorts were familiar with digital technologies and valued fast, personalized services, but their accounts differed in decision-making autonomy, social embeddedness, and evaluative practices. Generation Alpha participants more often positioned LLMs as an exploratory assistant within family-based decision structures, whereas Generation Z participants more frequently described comparing or verifying AI-generated outputs through other sources and social input. These patterns are better understood as different modes of credibility assessment and reliance than as simple differences in trust. The resulting GIFT ( Generational Interpretations of Future-oriented Technologies ) framework conceptualizes youth–AI interaction in tourism planning as context-dependent, with LLMs serving as cognitive support tools and potential co-creators. GIFT is presented as an exploratory framework grounded in this sample rather than as a universal theory. The study links human–AI interaction to the social contexts in which young people make travel decisions and offers implications for tourism professionals, educators, and AI developers.

title: Cultural dynamics of metadiscourse in Chinese mediation: a pragmatic approach to rapport management and conflict resolution
abstract: This study explores Chinese mediators’ strategic use of interactional metadiscourse for rapport management in family conflict resolution from a culturally localized pragmatic perspective. Drawing on five resolved family dispute cases from the Chinese television mediation program Baixing Tiaojie , the study integrates quantitative frequency counting of metadiscourse markers and qualitative pragmatic interpretation to unpack core linguistic patterns of Chinese mediation practice. The analysis reveals that Chinese mediators prioritize interactional metadiscourse to foster engagement over stance assertion, emphasizing active listening and participant orientation as central to effective communication and conflict resolution. The study verifies Spencer-Oatey’s Rapport Management Model and extends it by integrating indigenous Chinese cultural constructs centered on composite interests, affective bonds and collective welfare, relational face, legal codes and traditional etiquette norms, which collectively govern dynamic relational regulation throughout mediation procedures. Chinese mediators flexibly enhance, maintain, or readjust ties shaped by these factors to balance cultural norms and resolution goals. Contextualizing mediation discourse within Chinese socio-cultural conventions, this study clarifies how native value systems shape conflict talk and refines the cross-cultural explanatory capacity of rapport management frameworks. The findings highlight the indispensable function of culture-specific linguistic tactics in domestic mediation. Theoretically, the study enriches pragmatic research on conflict discourse by elaborating the linkage between cultural norms and metadiscursive practice. Practically, it delivers targeted references for domestic mediator training and cultural sensitivity cultivation in cross-cultural mediation scenarios.

title: Hegemonic articulation, paradigm incommensurability, and the discursive exclusion of Humanities and Social Science Research in the South African Open Science Policy 2026
abstract: The South African Open Science Policy 2026, published by the Department of Science, Technology, and Innovation, is formally committed to the democratisation of knowledge and epistemic equity. Yet a critical reading reveals that the Policy reproduces, through its own discursive architecture, the epistemological hierarchy it claims to dismantle. This article analyses the Policy as a discursive text, drawing on Laclau and Mouffe’s discourse theory and Foucault’s concept of the regime of truth to explain how a policy committed to democratisation can simultaneously enact epistemic exclusion. The primary argument is threefold. First, the Policy constructs “Open Science” as a nodal point around which a chain of equivalences is built from STEM-derived norms, including reproducibility, FAIR data principles, journal metrics, and natural science models of citizen science. Second, we argue that this hegemonic articulation reconstitutes a hidden antagonism between positivist and interpretivist epistemological traditions, reawakening a binary opposition that the paradigm wars of the twentieth century had ostensibly resolved. Third, the incommensurability between these traditions means that applying STEM-derived criteria universally to all research constitutes not evaluation but category error institutionalised as governance. Six dimensions of epistemological closure are examined: the reproducibility criterion, the FAIR data mandate, the marginalisation of CARE principles, the protective rather than epistemic treatment of indigenous knowledge, the structural absence of humanistic output forms, and the natural-science-centred design of the citizen science framework and its consequences for participatory research traditions. Five policy interventions are proposed through which the Policy’s stated commitment to epistemic equity could be made operational across the full disciplinary spectrum.

title: Cross-regional emission reduction based on government-enterprise-public collaboration in the construction industry
abstract: Excessive carbon emissions are recognized as a significant contributor to climate change and environmental degradation. Achieving carbon neutrality has become an imperative for sustainable development. This study examined carbon emission reduction mechanisms in the construction industry, focusing on collaborative efforts among key stakeholders to achieve balance, coordination, and sustainability in carbon emission control. Employing Stackelberg game theory, the study analyzed the strategic interactions among the government, enterprises, and the public in collaborative efforts to reduce carbon emissions. It explored their mutual influences from a macro-scale perspective, examining the strategic choices made by each stakeholder and the specific impacts of various parameters on the key decisions. The study employed MATLAB software to simulate the effects of six key driving policies on system evolution. This research aimed to provide a robust theoretical foundation and practical guidance for establishing cross-sector collaborative mechanisms to reduce carbon emissions from the construction industry.

title: Examining the role of social media influencers in shaping perceptions of sustainable supply chain practices in Egypt
abstract: Social media influencers have become central intermediaries in communicating corporate sustainability, yet it remains unclear how their characteristics shape stakeholder judgments about sustainable supply chains in emerging markets. To address this gap, the present study draws on the Elaboration Likelihood Model, informed by Stakeholder Theory, to examine how influencer credibility, engagement, perceived greenwashing risk, and economic constraints relate to trust, perceived supply chain transparency, and perceived adoption of sustainable practices in Egypt. Data were collected from 300 respondents, comprising both consumers and supply chain professionals, and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, multi-group analysis, and a bootstrapped mediation decomposition. The results show that credibility was positively associated with trust and transparency, whereas engagement functioned only as a weak peripheral cue; greenwashing risk, in turn, was negatively associated with trust. Although international influencers were rated as more trustworthy overall, local influencers were more strongly associated with trust and transparency when the message was context-specific, thereby revealing a credibility–context paradox. Economic constraints were related to perceived adoption through two opposing pathways: they were negatively associated with adoption directly but positively associated with it indirectly through trust and transparency; importantly, these relationships did not differ between consumers and professionals. Because the design is cross-sectional, the findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. Taken together, the study clarifies when and why influencer cues shape sustainability judgments and offers evidence-based guidance for influencer selection under economic pressure.

title: Integrating user values into climate science through co-production
abstract: Transdisciplinary approaches such as co-production are gaining prominence for their ability to improve the actionability of sciences and support solutions to complex societal problems. Yet effectively operationalizing co-production processes continues to be a significant challenge and a time-intensive effort. Particularly, there is limited understanding of how the various elements of science evolve during co-production, and how the values and priorities of non-academic societal partners can be robustly integrated into scientific research. In this manuscript, we examine the case study of a long-term transdisciplinary co-production project aimed at improving the credibility of climate modelling and developing actionable climate science for resource management. Drawing on a systematic longitudinal analysis of over 3 years of iterative engagements, we articulate a change pathway that describes how choices in scientific research evolved and transformed through interactions with non-academic partners. We also identify six distinct types of value negotiations that we confronted during the co-production engagements and provide examples of each negotiation-type, including cases where diverse values were easily assimilated, where practical challenges constrained value integration, where values were differently interpreted, as well as cases where values were incompatible. These results extend the philosophical discussions of value negotiations in climate science by providing empirical evidence on how iterative deliberations on values play out in practice. The change-pathway as well as the negotiation-types that we developed offer valuable lessons to other researchers, practitioners or boundary spanners, seeking to facilitate value negotiations and to make co-production processes more effective and efficient.

title: Negative word-of-mouth and potential customer churn in high-involvement services
abstract: Abstract This study examines how existing customers’ negative word-of-mouth is associated with potential customer churn and the re-spreading of negative word-of-mouth within high-involvement service contexts, adopting a service systems perspective. Through quantitative analysis of 308 interior decoration potential customer data using Structural Equation Modeling, we found that both perceived poor project performance and perceived unsatisfactory service performance significantly predict potential customer churn and the re-spreading of negative word-of-mouth. Results also reveal that perceived poor project performance has a stronger impact on the re-spreading of negative word-of-mouth than on potential customer churn, while perceived unsatisfactory service performance’s influence on potential customer churn slightly outweighs its effect on the re-spreading of negative word-of-mouth. Furthermore, demographic factors, such as gender and education level, play a moderating role in these relationships. This research enriches the literature on potential customer churn, modifies the Two-Step Flow of Communication theory, and elucidates negative word-of-mouth’s critical role as a feedback mechanism in service ecosystems.

title: Nonmaleficence, noninterference, and fidelity: environmental ethics in Gary Paulsen’s Hatchet (1986)
abstract: Abstract In the Anthropocene era, where human activities profoundly alter ecosystems, ethical reflections on human–nature relationships have become increasingly vital. Paul W. Taylor’s environmental ethics—particularly the principles of nonmaleficence, noninterference, and fidelity—provide a valuable framework for examining these relationships. Literature, especially young adult (YA) fiction, serves as a significant medium for shaping moral and ecological awareness among young readers. Despite its accessibility, YA nature writing has often been overlooked in ecocritical scholarship. This study explores the ethical dimensions of Gary Paulsen’s Hatchet (1986), a canonical YA wilderness survival novel that portrays the protagonist Brian Robeson’s encounters with animals, plants, and other nonhuman entities in the forests of northern Canada. Through the lens of Taylor’s Respect for Nature : A Theory of Environmental Ethics (1986), this study analyses how Brian’s experiences reflect the recognition of animal agency, human vulnerability, and adherence to ethical principles governing human–nonhuman interactions. The findings suggest that Paulsen’s narrative embodies a deep ecological sensibility that aligns with Taylor’s nonanthropocentric ethics. This research enriches the understanding of Hatchet (1986) and contributes to broader ecocritical discussions on environmental ethics in young adult literature.

title: The impact of public health events on individual physical health: taking the SARS epidemic as an example
abstract: This paper examines whether a short-lived public health shock affects subsequent physical health. We combine China Health and Nutrition Survey panel data from 1991 to 2009 with province-level SARS surveillance records and exploit cross-provincial variation in exposure to the 2003 SARS outbreak. The empirical design is a difference-in-differences specification with individual and survey-wave fixed effects. The estimates show that individuals in provinces more exposed to SARS experienced a decline in physical health after the outbreak. This result is robust to propensity-score adjusted DID specifications, alternative exposure measures, a city-population-based exposure denominator, alternative outcome coding, adult-sample restrictions, province-clustered inference, and leave-one-province-out checks. Event-study estimates show no clear pre-outbreak differential trend. Heterogeneity analysis suggests that the adverse effect is present for both women and men and is mainly concentrated among individuals with lower educational attainment. Channel evidence indicates that SARS exposure was associated with changes in drinking behavior and other health-related responses. The findings suggest that the health costs of public health emergencies extend beyond infection itself and may persist through behavioral and access-related adjustments.

title: Uncovering the impact of ownership types on tax aggressiveness in Indonesia
abstract: Abstract The purpose of this research is to empirically test and analyze the influence of ownership structure, including family ownership, management ownership, institutional ownership, state ownership, public ownership, foreign ownership, and concentrated ownership, on tax aggressiveness (ETR and CFETR). The ETR indicates a company’s behavior in reducing corporate taxes, while the CFETR denotes tax aggressiveness in terms of cash flow used to pay corporate taxes. These two measures can provide clues about whether a company is tax aggressive. This study is based on two theories—agency theory and socioemotional wealth theory. While agency theory is used to examine the impact of tax aggressiveness, socioemotional wealth theory examines the impact of family ownership on tax aggressiveness. This study employed a quantitative approach, using descriptive and inferential statistical analysis techniques to examine all companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) in 2023, yielding a total of 382 cross-sectional data units. The results of this study indicate that family ownership, management ownership, institutional ownership, state ownership, and foreign ownership have a significant effect, meaning that as the proportion of ownership increases, tax aggressiveness increases. In comparison, public ownership and concentrated ownership do not have a significant effect on tax aggressiveness. This study provides a new contribution to the capital market context in Indonesia, which comprehensively shows the types of ownership structures, namely family, managerial, institutional, state, public, foreign, and concentrated ownership, in relation to corporate aggressiveness. Future research should build on the results of this study to highlight the important role of shareholders in tax aggressiveness in Indonesia and other developing countries.

title: Representations of air tragedy in Chinese press: a corpus-driven critical discourse study
abstract: This article examines discourses surrounding air tragedies, aiming to investigate differences in ideological stances adopted by Chinese journalists toward three social actor groups associated with the crashed China Eastern Boeing 737. By integrating theories and methodologies from corpus linguistics and critical discourse studies, and employing corpus linguistics software, the study reveals that Chinese media constructs a positive representation of the “Our” group (the Chinese government and China Eastern Airlines) while framing the “Others” group (Boeing) negatively. It is argued that these representations function to systematically amplify public perception of responsibility and reliability toward the Chinese government and China Eastern Airlines, but risk and distrust toward Boeing. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the operational dynamics of the Discourse-Cognition-Society triangle, illustrating how the social structure delimits discursive strategies, and how discursive practice, in turn, actively intervenes to shape collective cognition and reproduce ideological positions.

title: Is green bond issuance an effective policy instrument to promote green growth? A global analysis
abstract: Green growth has become a central policy objective in response to escalating climate risks and environmental degradation; however, the role of specific financial instruments, particularly green bonds, in driving this transition remains insufficiently understood. While existing studies have examined various forms of green finance, the distinct role of green bonds remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by examining whether green bond issuance promotes green growth at the macro level. Using a panel dataset of 69 countries over the period 2010–2023, we employ a comprehensive Green Growth Index that captures multiple dimensions of sustainability, including resource efficiency, natural capital, green economic opportunities, and social inclusion. To ensure robust estimation, we apply a range of econometric techniques, including fixed effects (FE), Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, Panel-corrected standard errors, Two-step System GMMs, and Lewbel instrumental variable estimators. The results provide strong evidence that green bond issuance significantly enhances green growth at the global level, with a predominantly linear relationship. More interestingly, the sub-sample analyses reveal that green bond issuance significantly fosters green growth in advanced economies; however, its effect is not significant in emerging and developing economies. Further moderation analysis reveals that the effectiveness of green bonds increases with income levels and is strongly moderated by institutional quality, while financial development does not exhibit a statistically significant moderating effect. These findings suggest that although green bonds can serve as an effective policy instrument for promoting green growth, their impact critically depends on structural conditions, particularly institutional quality.

title: Governing inter-jurisdictional capital mobility: the role of regional cooperation in shaping firms’ cross-border investment
abstract: Abstract This study develops a new analytical framework for understanding how regional cooperation shapes cross-jurisdictional capital mobility. Using an original dataset that links news-based records of cooperative activities with firm-level evidence on non-local subsidiary establishments in China’s Yangtze River Delta (YRD) from 2010 to 2021, we show that regional cooperation plays a pivotal role in facilitating capital flows across administrative boundaries. The analysis identifies three governance mechanisms: reducing information asymmetries that heighten opportunity recognition, lowering institutional transaction costs rooted in bureaucratic fragmentation, and enabling knowledge spillovers that prompt innovation-driven capital reallocation. Socio-political cooperation—anchored in social capital and administrative coordination—exerts stronger influence on capital mobility than market-oriented initiatives, and formal agreements consistently outperform informal arrangements. By highlighting such differentiated effects, the study makes three contributions. It advances theories of capital mobility by placing regional cooperation at their core; it enriches regional integration scholarship through a comparative institutional perspective; and it offers policy-relevant insights for designing context-sensitive cooperative models to address spatial economic inequality. Overall, the findings illuminate how collaborative governance can reshape regional development trajectories within and beyond the Chinese context.

title: Rationality of public policies for spatial allocation of educational resources: case of primary schools in the west region of Cameroon
abstract: This study assesses the rationality of public policies for the spatial allocation of primary schools in the West region of Cameroon, in the context of ongoing crises and economic shocks. Using cross-sectional data of 2022 from the Ministry of Basic Education, the Central Bureau of Censuses and Population Studies., and the National Institute of Statistics, the analysis applies Ripley’s K function to examine whether the spatial distribution of public primary schools follows a clustered, random, or dispersed pattern relative to population distribution. This spatial statistical approach is complemented by Monte Carlo simulations to test the significance of observed patterns. The results show that, while school locations are generally aligned with population concentration, some districts exhibit random spatial allocation. These findings suggest the need for more rational and demand-driven school placement policies, particularly through prioritizing densely populated areas to improve access and educational outcomes.

title: How green brands build commitment: a cognition–affect–conation perspective from the new energy vehicle market
abstract: As China’s new energy vehicle (NEV) market shifts from rapid adoption to intensified competition, sustaining long-term consumer–brand relationships has become increasingly critical. Drawing on the cognition–affect–conation (CAC) framework, this study develops and tests a model explaining how green brand commitment is formed in the post-purchase stage. Specifically, seven cognitive antecedents, including three dimensions of green self-congruity (actual self, ideal self, and social self) and four dimensions of green brand authenticity (continuity, originality, reliability, and naturalness), are examined as predictors of green brand attachment. Green brand attachment is positioned as the affective mediator, while brand commitment represents the conative outcome. Perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE) is further introduced as a moderator. PLS-SEM analysis of survey data collected from 216 NEV users in Guangzhou reveals that all cognitive antecedents except ideal self-congruity have significant positive effects on green brand attachment. Green brand attachment positively influences brand commitment and mediates the effects of several cognitive antecedents on brand commitment. Moreover, PCE strengthens the effect of brand attachment on brand commitment. This study extends green branding research from the adoption stage to the post-purchase relationship stage and provides empirical evidence for the applicability of the CAC framework in the NEV context. The findings offer practical guidance for NEV firms seeking to foster enduring brand commitment through identity alignment, authenticity enhancement, and differentiated psychological segmentation strategies.

title: The evolution of information ecosystems: a macro-exploratory analysis of digital intelligence empowerment
abstract: Generative AI and agent-based systems are reshaping how information is produced, circulated, and validated, making synthetic content and model hallucinations increasingly routine features of contemporary information environments. While Web 2.0 perspectives explain connectivity, participation, and diffusion well, they are less able to account for ecosystems in which model-mediated generation transforms informational objects and shifts value toward verification and provenance. The article’s central claim is that information ecosystems are undergoing a macro-level transition from networked connectivity to generative symbiosis, a condition in which human actors and generative systems recursively co-produce informational outputs, and in which verification, rather than attention, becomes the ecosystem’s central organizing constraint. To theorize this transition, the article conceptualizes digital intelligence as the coupling of ubiquitous digital sensing and generative agency, and links information ecology with algorithmic epistemology. Empirically, the study adopts an exploratory qualitative and abductive design based on two analytically complementary Chinese cases spanning public governance and market production: Hangzhou’s City Brain 3.0 and Haier’s COSMOPlat/HIMOS, which jointly capture top-down administrative and bottom-up market logics and thus support a macro-exploratory analysis of systemic evolution. Drawing on triangulated technical, policy, and public-discourse materials, and with explicit reflexive attention to promotional bias in self-disclosed sources, the analysis traces how this transition operates through two coupling mechanisms. Semantic alignment translates unstructured inputs into machine-actionable representations, in a statistical rather than intentional sense, and agent-based coordination delegates matching, scheduling, and negotiation tasks to bounded autonomous agents. The same mechanisms generate three interrelated paradoxes concerning power, materiality, and verification, read here as dialectical contradictions rooted in the dual constitution of digital intelligence as technological morphology and intelligent function. As a theory-building, macro-exploratory study grounded in two cases and largely public materials, the article advances analytical rather than causal claims. It concludes by proposing a reverse-reconstruction governance approach that shifts attention from downstream content harms alone to the upstream epistemic and institutional conditions under which outputs become intelligible, credible, and actionable, and operationalizes this approach through a baseline epistemic audit covering provenance integrity, uncertainty disclosure, human-fallback rules, model-change traceability, and drift and flattening monitoring, alongside green-computing constraints and human oversight along the information-production chain. Overall, the article offers a framework for explaining how digital intelligence is reconfiguring information ecosystems and for informing more accountable, transparent, and adaptive governance responses to AI-mediated information environments.

title: Medicine with a simple cure - walk, meditate, and pray to reduce stress and boost immunity
abstract: Human well-being, overall and immune system health, is the result of many variables, and an individual’s adaptive abilities. By understanding the connections between everyday choices, the laws governing the body, and additionally considering the social, psycho-emotional, cultural, spiritual, and environmental aspects of humanity, people can avoid disease themselves. Moreover, for the chronically ill, it could also increase their chances of survival or even return to health by raising their awareness and implementing some of the possible and easy-to-use techniques. Immunology, as an advanced field of medicine, is still evolving and can be difficult to understand for many people, including scientists specializing in other disciplines. In the face of a rapid increase in the incidence of both civilization-related and autoimmune diseases, this work aims to bridge the gap between science and everyday human life. Looking for a more human-centered dimension of medicine and immunology science, the impact of easy-to-apply daily practices on health and the immune system is worth exploring. In this context, authors present stress reduction techniques such as meditation and prayer, as well as ways to enhance their effects through activities in nature, for example, calming walks or pilgrimages. Similarly, the intricacies of many traditions, including religion, remained mysterious despite being known for years. These activities are seldom covered in the literature on immune system health, and this study helps readers gain a better understanding of these relationships. It can also help to restore some of the heritage of preventive healthcare in support of modern, conventional treatments.

title: The City and the Plow: urban anxieties and the origins of the American Country Life Movement
abstract: During the early twentieth century, often referred to as the “golden age” of American agriculture, President Theodore Roosevelt initiated the Country Life Movement, a campaign aimed at rural reform. This seemingly paradoxical historical development constitutes the central inquiry of this article: why did Progressive-era reformers advocate for rural reforms precisely at a time when agricultural conditions were improving? Utilizing critical discourse analysis of primary sources from the 1890s through the 1920s, this study contends that the movement’s driving force was not rural poverty but rather urban anxieties. Specifically, there was a concern that agricultural prosperity might accelerate rural depopulation, diminish the countryside’s function as a demographic and moral reservoir, and ultimately threaten the stability of industrial urban centers. Consequently, the Country Life Movement should be understood not as a reaction to agrarian distress but as a proactive urban strategy aimed at securing food supplies, population stability, and social order. By reframing urban concerns as the primary causal factor, highlighting ecological, socio-racial, and institutional aspects neglected in previous scholarship, and situating the American case within a comparative global context of urban-rural governance, this article provides a significant reinterpretation of one of the Progressive Era’s most understudied reform initiatives.

title: Cultural dynamics in merger and acquisition (M&A): examining the strategic competencies- performance link in Pakistani manufacturing firms using PLS-SEM
abstract: Despite extensive research on Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A), few empirical studies integrate strategic management perspectives with organizational culture, particularly regarding the Moderating role of M&A culture in emerging markets. This study fills this research gap by investigating whether M&A Culture moderates the relationship between strategic M&A Competencies (function, learning, and capabilities) and M&A performance in Pakistan’s manufacturing sector. A sample of 237 managers from manufacturing companies that had recently engaged in M&As provided the data for this study through surveys; the data was analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The study found a statistically significant positive relationship between Strategic M&A Competencies and M&A Performance. Moreover, the study found that M&A Culture is a significant moderator that enhances the effect of strategic M&A competencies on M&A outcomes. Theoretically, this study combines cultural contingency theory and dynamic capability theory. Practically, the study provides guidance to managers to optimize their strategic competences in high-context cultural environments. This research is one of the first to provide empirical evidence from an emerging market context to address the institutional voids often ignored in western-centric M&A literature.

title: Digital divide, social development, and gender disparity: a critical analysis of the National Education Policy 2020: ways forward
abstract: Standing at the crux of a situation when digitization, corporate monopoly, media oligopoly, etc. have become the new “normal” of a capitalized worldview, the education system in India has also undergone a sea change. The commodification of education has made the divide, or the gap between the rural and urban populations, the rich and the poor, the backward and the upfront or mainstream learners, gender disparity and gender mainstreaming more apparent. In the name of academic excellence and academic collaboration, a host of pressing market imperatives or competitive edge factors are imposed on educational institutions, which is symptomatic of a neo liberalization process where education is no longer an ideology but rather a commodity. And to hide this economic and political rationality behind liberalizing education under the garb of “development,” a series of changes in terms of structuring and restructuring variables to decide the performance of academia in the national and international market have been put in place. The intensification of academic work, reinventing teaching-learning methodologies, research, and academic service, and the increase in various measurements of productivity, efficiency, quality, and accountability have placed new demands on academics to perform productively and reinvent themselves. This study has identified the consequences of these material and affective changes in the Indian higher education system—as is evident in the New Education Policy 2020—and how conducive it is for bringing in social and economic development for all, especially for the Indian rural population. Also, the study will look into the “development” paradigm from the prism of gender equity and sustainable inclusive growth, where education plays a key role in bringing in equitable distribution of wealth and resources. The research method used in this study is historical analysis, semiotic analysis and discourse analysis. The findings of the study clearly indicate that the primary and secondary education system in rural India, especially Govt. or Govt.-aided school have to be upgraded enough to accommodate digitization in the teaching-learning method. Indian Govt. must allocate more funds for making education accessible and affordable to the rural population.

title: Collecting probabilistic goods: a framework for sequential decision-making based on the Coupon Collector’s Problem
abstract: Abstract In this work, we investigate consumers’ sequential decision-making behavior under the setting of collection-based probabilistic selling. We formulate the sequential purchasing process as a draw-level Markov Decision Process (MDP) built on the classical Coupon Collector’s Problem. The Bellman recursion can be reduced exactly to a stage-level stopping problem, yielding an explicit value function and optimal stopping rule for forward-looking collectors. We further extend the analysis by characterizing collection goals (complete vs. partial) and quantifying the impact of consumer heterogeneity, demonstrating how risk preferences shape optimal stopping decisions. In our extensions, we analyze duplicate salvage, pity systems, and finite budget constraints and complement these results with discussions of batch purchasing and a demand-side completion premium. Finally, we provide numerical illustrations of the analytical results under selected parameter settings. This work provides a tractable analytical benchmark for understanding sequential stopping decisions in collection-based probabilistic selling.

title: Athlete gender visibility, emotional narratives, and audience engagement in CCTV News’s Olympic short-video coverage on Douyin: an empirical analysis
abstract: Short-form video platforms have become important channels for major sports-event coverage, but empirical evidence remains limited regarding how athletes are presented, how emotions are organized, and how these features relate to audience engagement in specific institutional accounts. This study analyzes 219 short-video posts published by the official China Central Television (CCTV) News account on Douyin during the 2024 Paris Olympic Games. Content analysis, t-tests, and regression analysis were used to examine mention-based athlete gender visibility, emotional narratives, and three platform-displayed engagement indicators: likes, comments, and shares. The results show no statistically significant difference between female and male athletes in mention frequency, indicating relative balance only at the level of being named. Athlete mention frequency was not significantly associated with likes, comments, or shares. Emotional narratives were not directly associated with higher engagement, but posts using emotional narratives contained significantly more athlete mentions. Emotional narrative also positively moderated the relationship between mention frequency and shares, although not the relationships with likes or comments. These findings suggest that, within this single-account and single-platform case, mention frequency is a potential narrative resource rather than an engagement outcome in itself, and its association with content diffusion depends partly on emotional framing. The conclusions should not be generalized to all Chinese mainstream media or interpreted as evidence of complete gender equality in athlete portrayal.

title: Three decades on: pathways and barriers to practical reconciliation and psychosocial reconstruction in Rwanda after the genocide against the Tutsi
abstract: Three decades after the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, Rwanda continues to navigate the complex and evolving process of psychosocial reconstruction and practical reconciliation among survivors, former perpetrators, and their descendants. Despite substantial national and community-based efforts to advance reconciliation, restorative justice, and psychosocial transformation, many individuals continue to experience profound difficulties, including depression, trauma-related distress, anxiety, social mistrust and unresolved grief that impede sustainable recovery, social cohesion, and meaningful coexistence. Important gaps therefore remain in understanding the opportunities and obstacles that shape psychosocial reconstruction and reconciliation in post-genocide settings. The present study addressed these gaps by exploring the pathways and barriers to reconciliation and psychosocial reconstruction in the Rwandan context. Using a qualitative design, we conducted 32 semi-structured interviews with genocide survivors ( n = 5), ex-prisoners ( n = 5), and local leaders ( n = 5) in Nyamagabe District, complemented by three focus-group discussions involving both survivors and ex-prisoners ( n = 7), only survivors ( n = 5) and only perpetrators ( n = 5). Data were analysed inductively using thematic analysis. The findings indicate that post-genocide psychosocial reconstruction and reconciliation have been facilitated by grassroots initiatives particularly traditional justice mechanisms and reinforced by psychosocial programmes led by the government and its partners. However, persistent barriers remain, including ongoing psychosocial difficulties (anxiety, trauma, social mistrust and shame), intergenerational trauma, and limited access to psychosocial services, all of which hinder sustainable social transformation. Overall, the study reveals that practical reconciliation is a dynamic, non-linear process in which community-based engagement, psychosocial healing, and identity reconstruction drive positive change, while structural challenges continue to compromise these gains. These findings suggest that sustained partnership and collaboration among policymakers, mental health professionals, peacebuilders, and academics are essential to advance lasting psychosocial reconstruction, reconciliation, and social cohesion in post-genocide contexts.

title: Artificial Intelligence for environmental sustainability: a systematic review of applications, impact pathways, and governance implications
abstract: The escalating urgency of climate change and environmental degradation has intensified demand for scalable solutions that strengthen system resilience and support progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. Artificial intelligence offers substantial potential to enhance environmental monitoring and decision support, yet the evidence remains dispersed across domains, methods, and industry contexts. This study provides a systematic review of AI for environmental sustainability, synthesizing evidence from 493 identified journal articles. The review examines how AI is applied to environmental sustainability and identifies the main barriers affecting its outcomes. It uses an impact-pathway framework to explain how institutional capacity and governance shape the environmental effects of AI deployment. Findings indicate that AI applications concentrate in infrastructure-intensive sectors, particularly transportation, communication, and electric, gas, and sanitary services, followed by cross-cutting domains spanning IT-enabled environmental applications, water systems, and resource management. Across sectors, supervised and unsupervised learning, deep learning, forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization-oriented approaches are most prevalent, while text-intensive approaches such as natural language processing (NLP) and sequence mining remain comparatively underexplored. The review shows that net sustainability outcomes depend on the balance between measurable environmental gains and the operational and lifecycle burdens of AI deployment. The proposed framework identifies governance capacity, Green AI engineering, and infrastructure choices as factors that shape this balance.

title: Revisiting the policy on Philippine Higher Education Internationalization: Communicative rationality, neoliberalism, and emancipatory possibilities
abstract: This article offers a philosophical re-examination of the Commission on Higher Education’s Memorandum Order No. 55, s. 2016 (CMO 55), commonly framed as the policy on the “Internationalization of Philippine Higher Education.” It argues that CMO 55 does not merely outline internationalization as a technical agenda but discursively aligns it with neoliberal priorities by framing global competitiveness, human capital formation, and quality assurance as central purposes of higher education. Drawing on Jürgen Habermas’s Theory of Communicative Action, the study analyzes how CMO 55 interweaves communicative and strategic rationalities, appropriating the language of cooperation, stakeholder participation, and quality to legitimize market-oriented reforms and performance-driven governance. The analysis of selected provisions and coded themes shows that, while CMO 55 presents itself as promoting intercultural exchange, institutional collaboration, and enhanced academic standards, its discourse functions as strategic communication that normalizes labor-market alignment, institutional differentiation, and global benchmarking as taken-for-granted policy imperatives. Universities are constructed as competitive providers in a global education marketplace, and students and faculty are positioned as mobile, self-optimizing subjects. From a Habermasian perspective, communicative action is not realized within the policy; rather, it serves as a normative benchmark that highlights a gap between the rhetoric of dialoge and participation and the policy’s underlying strategic functions. In this sense, CMO 55 reinforces broader neoliberal patterns in which education is increasingly commodified and oriented toward economic utility, with democratic, civic, and humanistic purposes pushed to the margins.

title: Psychological and behavioral determinants of in-game purchase intention: the role of flow experience, addiction and e-WOM
abstract: The main purpose of this study is to determine the antecedents of online game purchase intention. The theoretical background of the research is based on the Flow Experience Theory. In this context, the study examines the relationships between flow experience, online game addiction, smartphone addiction, stickiness, e-WOM, and in-game purchase intention. Data were obtained from 870 participants via an online survey using the convenience sampling technique. To test the hypotheses of the research, PLS-SEM was employed using the SmartPLS software. The results of the study show that flow experience and e-WOM are the variables that directly affect in-game purchase intention. In addition, flow experience was found to have a significant effect on online game addiction, smartphone addiction, and stickiness. Furthermore, the effects of flow experience, online game addiction, smartphone addiction, and stickiness on e-WOM were statistically confirmed. By identifying the determinants of in-game purchase intention, this study makes a theoretical contribution to the literature on consumer (user/player) behavior in digital gaming environments. The findings specifically demonstrate how flow experience, different forms of addiction, stickiness, and e-WOM are associated with in-game purchase intention, thereby advancing scholarly discussions on consumer behavior within the digital gaming context. From a practical standpoint, the results provide guidance for game and application developers, marketing professionals, and managers in designing strategies aimed at enhancing user engagement and purchase-related outcomes. Finally, future research is encouraged to examine the indirect effects of the variables included in this study on in-game purchase intention.

title: Designing fairness: best practices for gender-sensitive development of cognitive ability tests in recruitment
abstract: Abstract Psychological tests play a pivotal role in high-stakes decisions such as recruitment, yet traditional development guidelines concentrate fairness work downstream — at test administration and post hoc statistical bias correction — while offering little concrete guidance for the design stage, where constructs are defined and operationalized. Drawing on constructivist and organizational justice theories, we argue that a “bias by design” arises when unexamined default assumptions narrow construct representation, systematically disadvantaging groups before any item is administered. We develop this for cognitive ability tests, which exhibit the largest subgroup differences among common selection instruments and routinely rely on figural matrices as proxies for general ability, thereby disadvantaging women. We contrast procedural justice (standardized administration) with distributive justice (equitable score distributions), clarifying that the latter applies to a principled class of constructs — latent and content-general, such as fluid intelligence — for which content-linked group differences signal construct-irrelevant variance rather than true differences. To address this gap, we adapt Stanford’s Gendered Innovations framework and demonstrate its application through the Modularer Kurzintelligenztest (M-KIT; Dantlgraber et al., 2015). Fairness can be addressed at three hierarchically ordered levels, where higher levels constrain lower ones: the theoretical model (broadening construct representation), the task format (removing construct-irrelevant demands), and the item (differential item functioning as final refinement, not primary remedy). We distill practical recommendations for embedding distributive justice early, including questioning default assumptions and documenting fairness deliberations. Our approach reframes fairness not as a trade-off but as integral to validity, offering a roadmap for more inclusive assessments.

title: Carbon lever and green gear: how firm-level carbon finance sparks green innovation efficiency in manufacturing
abstract: In the face of mounting pressure on global initiatives to combat climate change, the question of how to capitalize on the opportunity presented by green transformation has become a pressing concern. Unlike the concept of green finance, carbon finance (CF) is a specific means dedicated to reducing greenhouse gases. Its essence lies in emerging financial tools based on strict technical accounting, with carbon emissions as the primary commodity and reliance on the financial market. Therefore, based on the data of A-share listed manufacturing enterprises from 2009 to 2023, this study constructs a carbon finance measurement at the firm level and explores the causal relationship between CF and the green innovation efficiency (GIE) of manufacturing enterprises. The findings indicate that: (1) Enterprises’ CF can boost the GIE. High-tech manufacturing companies, as well as those in the mature and declining stages, exhibit this boosting influence in particular. (2) The development of CF can enhance the GIE of enterprises through two main channels: increasing the proportion of senior executives with environmental backgrounds and improving the short-term debt-paying ability of enterprises. (3) The impact of CF is moderated both positively and negatively by the degree of digital integration (Dig) and financing constraints (Sa). The level of Dig and Sa play a positive and negative moderation role in the impact of carbon finance. The results provide a reference for the application of carbon financial tools in the entity economy from a micro perspective.

title: Latency and liability: rethinking civil responsibility in low-latency human–AI systems under EU law
abstract: The European Union’s emerging AI regulatory framework combines extensive ex ante governance with comparatively fragmented civil liability mechanisms. While the AI Act establishes obligations concerning human oversight, logging and transparency, and the recast Product Liability Directive extends strict liability to software and digital products, the allocation of responsibility in real-time human–AI interaction environments remains legally uncertain. Using doctrinal legal analysis of EU legislation, case law, and speed-sensitive sectoral regulation, this article asks how temporal constraints on human intervention should inform existing civil liability categories. This article argues that system latency should be treated as a legally relevant variable in EU civil liability analysis. Latency conditions whether meaningful human intervention is realistically possible, influences how foreseeability should be assessed, and helps identify which actor is best positioned to prevent harm. Building on EU legislation, recent scholarship and the regulatory treatment of algorithmic trading under MiFID II, the article proposes a latency-sensitive control test structured around four factors: intervention window, override and fail-safe capacity, ex ante configuration and lifecycle control, and temporal traceability. The factors are neither cumulative nor equally weighted; they perform distinct factual, preventive and evidential functions. The test is not a freestanding cause of action or an EU-wide negligence rule, but an interpretive framework for mapping temporally relevant facts onto the applicable liability regime. The test offers courts and regulators a practical doctrinal tool for allocating responsibility in low-latency human–AI systems without departing from the existing architecture of EU liability law. The article thereby proposes an operational framework for assessing control and allocating responsibility in time-constrained human–AI interactions under existing EU law.

title: The nexus between climate change, natural resources, and small arms demand: a panel data analysis
abstract: Building on previous research that links the adverse societal impacts of climate change to a heightened risk of armed conflict, this study explores a fundamental underlying mechanism of this relationship―the potential for conflict parties to anticipate and prepare for these risks by augmenting their armed capacities. However, the extent of this increase is likely contingent upon the natural resource conditions present in a given country. Climate change may intensify violent competition for resources, particularly in countries characterized by either resource abundance or scarcity, further driving the demand for arms. This research provides compelling evidence supporting this hypothesis, especially in the context of developing countries, which are disproportionately affected by the intersection of climate change, resource competition, fragile governance, and recurrent security threats.

title: Micro-competition and macro-coevolution: knowledge-production dynamics of China’s climate-change issues under policy-led mode 3
abstract: How public attention enters knowledge production on climate change is central to understanding the relationship among scientific agendas, social demand and policy orientation. Using monthly data from December 2011 to November 2025, this study combines Baidu Index, Google Trends, CNKI title searches and Web of Science title searches to examine the dynamic relationship between search attention and article output. We first use the single title term “climate change” as an exploratory micro-level sample, then extend the Chinese analysis to an eleven-keyword macro issue system for ecological and environmental governance, with an eight-keyword specification and an international aggregate benchmark used for robustness and comparison. The results suggest that the single Chinese “climate change” term is associated with a negative coupling pattern, whereas the eleven-keyword macro system shows a positive relationship; the eight-keyword robustness specification preserves this direction. We therefore propose a cautious, exploratory interpretation of policy-led Mode 3: policy discourse and planning cycles may reorganize issue boundaries and naming entries, so that micro-level keywords may appear to compete while the macro issue system continues to coevolve. The argument is not that policy events provide a single causal explanation, but that multiple layers of evidence are consistent with a policy-axis mechanism of issue reorientation.

title: The nexus between spatial changes to paratexts and the reception of literary translation: a case study of Xi You Ji
abstract: In the realm of Translation Studies, paratext has been widely acknowledged as a mediator between texts and readers. However, very little attention has been paid to the area of the analysis of the paratextual evolution of the same translation and its impact on the reception of the work. Given the paucity of research in this area, this study employs Genette’s paratextual theory and aims to identify the spatial changes to paratexts in Xi You Ji ’s English translations, and to discuss their effect on the reception of the works. For this purpose, the readers’ reviews posted on Amazon on Arthur Waley’s and Julia Lovell’s works were gathered and examined. The findings of this study reveal that the transformation of book covers can affect the purchase decision of prospective readers to a large extent. The shift from epitext to peritext acts as an endorsement of the work and helps narrow the distance between readers and a foreign literary classic. The addition of an allographic introduction originated from academic research has a similar effect. The analysis further unveils that adding an allographic introduction raises the chances of giving the plot away in advance. This study provides a new research paradigm for reception studies. By highlighting the nuanced role of paratexts, it contributes to a broader discussion on the reception of literary translation and the overseas spread of influential classics.

title: Designing walkable streets: Exploring nonlinear effects of street-level built environment on older adults’ walking intention
abstract: The growing trend of older adults aging in their long-term residential settings has increased the demand for built environment designs that promote mobility, safety, and social engagement. Streets, as accessible and ubiquitous public spaces, play a critical role in shaping older adults’ walking intention and overall well-being, highlighting the importance of age-friendly street design. However, the relationship between the street-level built environment and older adults’ walking intention remains underexplored, especially regarding potential nonlinear effects. This study employed the DeepLabV3 semantic segmentation model to extract street-level built environment features from street view images. Older adults’ walking intention was quantitatively assessed by applying the Microsoft TrueSkill algorithm to convert pairwise image comparisons into ranked scores. Integrating a Gradient Boosting Decision Tree model with SHAP analysis, we examined the nonlinear and interaction effects of street-level built environment features on walking intention. Results showed that: (1) street-level built environment features were stronger determinants of older adults’ walking intention than socioeconomic factors, with green view index exerting the greatest influence; (2) the effects of street-level features exhibited nonlinear patterns, mainly power or exponential functions, with a threshold at GVI = 0.48 beyond which marginal gains diminished; (3) GVI, pedestrian path ratio, and colour richness were positively correlated with older adults’ walking intention, while building-to-street ratio, proportion of walls, and crowd concentration index showed negative correlations; and (4) significant interaction effects were observed among street-level built environment features. This study advances theoretical understanding of how microscale built environment shapes human behavior through nonlinear and synergistic mechanisms, providing actionable insights for designing age-friendly and walkable communities.

title: More minds, more learning: integrating peer learning with lectures to boost conceptual understanding in medical education
abstract: Lectures as a primary method for knowledge transmission often fail to foster deep conceptual understanding among students. To investigate whether enabling peer discussion enhances learning outcomes, 88 undergraduate students from a Saudi medical school were randomly assigned to four experimental conditions: a lecture-only group, a peer-learning-only group, a peer-learning-followed-by-lecture group, and a lecture-followed-by-peer-learning group. A comprehensive concept retrieval test was administered before and after the intervention to isolate and evaluate the specific instructional effects of each approach separately. Pre-test scores showed no significant differences among the four groups, confirming successful randomization and equivalent baseline knowledge. Post-intervention test results revealed substantial variations in performance across the groups. Mean test scores (with standard deviations) were: lecture-only = 23.09 (2.84), peer-learning-only = 31.05 (3.94), lecture-then-peer-learning = 47.30 (5.75), and peer-learning-then-lecture = 49.55 (7.06). Statistical analysis demonstrated that combining lectures with peer learning significantly outperformed single-method instructional approaches ( p < 0.001 for both comparative evaluations), regardless of the order in which the two methods were implemented. Furthermore, peer learning in isolation produced significantly higher test scores compared to the traditional lecture-only strategy ( p = 0.05). These findings demonstrate that integrating peer learning with traditional lectures yields superior academic achievement compared to relying on lectures alone. Furthermore, the strong performance observed in the peer-learning-only condition highlights its promise as a highly effective standalone pedagogical strategy for medical education.

title: Social and technical drivers of traditional craftspeople’s continuance intention to use AI-generated content systems: a mixed SEM–fsQCA study
abstract: This study investigates the interplay between social and technological factors affecting traditional craftspeople’s ongoing willingness to utilize generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) tools, specifically text-based models and image generators, aiming to elucidate the cognitive and affective mechanisms underlying their behavior, grounded in social influence theory and the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) model. This study uses a mixed-methods approach combining partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to analyze data from 209 traditional craftspeople in China. The study examined the linear and group effects of social influences and technical attributes on perceived value, trust, and willingness to sustain use. PLS-SEM results indicate that industry support, peer influence, content quality, and performance significantly enhance craftspeople’s perceived value and trust, which, in turn, positively affect their continued willingness to use. The effects of social identity and platform technology on trust are not significant. Mediation effect analysis indicated that perceived value partially mediated multiple paths, whereas trust more often appeared as a full mediator. fsQCA further revealed six sufficiently grouped paths with high consistency, which were categorized into three dominant mechanism types: content–performance compensation-driven, identity–peer reinforcement-driven, and social endorsement–technology synergy. This study integrates and applies social influence theory and the SOR model to the study of AIGC adoption behavior among traditional craftspeople. The results demonstrate that for culturally embedded and digitally vulnerable traditional craftspeople, social and technical cues operate through distinct cognitive and affective routes, with trust playing a particularly central role in driving continuance intention. This provides a nuanced view of the behavioral drivers within this traditional group of craftspeople.

title: Rethinking book–tax conformity: a systematic exploration of methods, debates, and policy trade-offs
abstract: Abstract Book-tax conformity remains a debated issue in accounting, taxation, and public policy. While some experts argue that aligning financial and tax reporting improves transparency and limits opportunities for earnings management or tax avoidance, others caution against undermining the distinct goals of accounting and taxation. This study offers a systematic review of the literature, critically examining measurement methods, theoretical and empirical debates, and policy trade-offs discussed in the field. Using the PRISMA approach, the review ensures quality and analyzes publications from Scopus Q1–Q4 journals spanning 2000 to 2024. The results highlight differences in measurement approaches, gaps in cross-country analysis, and the need for a more comprehensive framework that includes institutional and behavioral factors. This paper contributes by synthesizing scattered research, identifying areas needing further exploration, and proposing a research agenda to support more informed and balanced policymaking in corporate tax regulation.

title: Gen Z’s digital activism: youth-led protests and political crises in Asia
abstract: This study examines the role of Generation Z (Gen Z) in shaping political crises and social protests across 20 Asian countries between 2019 and 2025, with a focus on the dynamics of digital activism. Through qualitative content and sentiment analysis using natural language processing (NLP) methods, this research uncovers how Gen Z mobilizes leaderless, digitally driven movements against corruption, economic inequality, and authoritarian governance. Findings reveal common cross-country patterns, including hybrid online–offline tactics, symbolic acts of resistance, and decentralized leadership structures. While social media amplifies youth voices and accelerates mobilization, it simultaneously increases vulnerability to state repression, producing divergent outcomes ranging from leadership change to reinforced authoritarian control. The discussion highlights critical implications for governance, digital rights, and youth political participation, underscoring the urgent need for inclusive policies that address both democratic engagement and socioeconomic grievances. This article contributes to the broader understanding of post-digital activism and its transformative potential in the Global South.

title: The global validation and results of an assessment tool for urban age-friendliness: A great leap forward towards an age-friendly world
abstract: Abstract Age-friendly cities around the world aim to enhance the quality of life of older people. A network of like-minded cities and communities promotes the exchange of best practices, but faces challenges due to varying socio-economic and cultural contexts, which affects comparability and usability of shared information and limits mutual learning. The Age-Friendly Cities and Communities Questionnaire (AFCCQ) serves as a tool for assessment of cities’ age-friendliness. This study validates the AFCCQ’s cross-cultural applicability in ten countries (Italy, Poland, North Macedonia, Romania, the Netherlands, Australia, Turkey, Russia, Japan, and Israel) through data from 4648 participants, testing measurement invariance with structural equation modelling. Finally, descriptive statistics provided a baseline comparison between countries. Results confirm that the AFCCQ enables a uniform assessment across countries, facilitating meaningful international comparisons. Findings aid global entities like the World Health Organization in fostering age-friendly environments and assist policymakers in developing effective age- friendly policies.

title: Globalization and the gender income gap: evidence from the export technology complexity in China
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of the improvement of the position in the manufacturing global value chain (GVC) on the gender wage gap, drawing on both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Using export technology complexity to measure the extent of GVC integration across Chinese provinces, this study combines provincial-level data with individual-level information from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS). This study finds that the occupational gender wage gap tends to decrease with increasing the embedding of the manufacturing global value chain position, with more pronounced effects observed in in low-skilled, low-wage, and underdeveloped areas. The mechanism is that the integration into global value chains enhances female human capital, reduces the gender gap in market labor participation and traditional gender stereotypes, but this does not mean that the status and awareness of women's career advancement have been further improved. These results offer valuable policy insights for advancing the goal of common prosperity.

title: Socio-economic transformation and inequality in South Africa: a regional analysis
abstract: Socio-economic transformation is the process through which the main sources of national income, output, and employment shift away from primary sector activities such as agriculture towards more productive sectors like manufacturing and services. This transition is widely recognised as a critical driver of rapid and sustained economic growth. However, since the seminal contributions of Simon Kuznets, it has been broadly argued that structural transformation may initially be associated with rising income inequality, a phenomenon known as the developer’s dilemma. As a result, in the short run, countries undergoing transformation may face a trade-off between promoting economic growth and managing inequality. When policymakers are confronted with the trade-off, concerns over widening inequality may sometimes lead them to slow down, alter or even reverse reforms aimed at advancing socio-economic transformation. The study aims to estimate the effects of the socio-economic transformation (SET) on inequality in South Africa at the regional level to determine the extent to which regional economies are socioeconomically transforming. This is motivated by high regional disparities in development outcomes across the nine provinces. The Driscoll–Kraay Fixed Effects regression was adopted given that the regional panels were characterised by cross-sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity using Statistics South Africa regionally disaggregated data from 2008Q1 to 2022Q4.
